Stanley Smith Stevens (4 November 1906 – 18 January 1973) was an American psychologist. He founded Harvard's Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory and introduced Stevens' power law. He also wrote an important textbook, the 1400+ page "Handbook of Experimental Psychology" (1951). He was born in Ogden, Utah to Stanely and Adeline (Smith) Stevens and educated in LDS-affiliated schools in Salt Lake City, Utah. He spent much of his childhood in the household of his grandfather Orson Smith. At the death of his parents in 1924, he spent the next 3 years on an LDS mission in Switzerland and Belgium. He attended the University of Utah from 1927 to 1929 and Stanford University for the next two years, graduating with an A.B. in psychology from Stanford in 1931. He married Maxine Leonard in 1930 and had a son, Peter Smith, in 1936.

Stanley Tookie Williams III (December 29, 1953 – December 13, 2005) was an American murderer and co-founder of a street gang, the Crips who are rivals of the Bloods. He was born in New Orleans, Louisiana. In 1959, he moved to Los Angeles, California, where in 1970 he stole a car, for which he was convicted and sent to juvenile hall. He and Raymond Washington (1953–1979) founded street gang the Crips in 1971 in Los Angeles. Williams shot four people dead in Los Angeles in 1979 during robberies he committed. The events were caught on film by surveillance cameras. Later that year he was convicted of four counts of first degree murder and two counts of robbery. He was sentenced to death and was executed by lethal injection at San Quentin State Prison, California. He was a Christian at the time of his death. He was called by his middle name Tookie.

Stanley Price (12 August 1931 – 28 February 2019) was a British novelist and playwright. He wrote for the theatre, movie and television. He was born in London. Price was known for writing the screenplays for Arabesque, Gold and Shout at the Devil. For television, he wrote A Royal Scandal. Price was born in London. Price died on 28 February 2019 in London at the age of 87.

Stanley Tigerman (September 20, 1930 – June 3, 2019) was an American architect, theorist and designer. He was an important architect in Chicago, Illinois. Tigerman's best known designs include the Five Polytechnic Institutes in Bangladesh, the Illinois Holocaust Museum and Education Center in Skokie, Illinois, the Illinois Regional Library for the Blind and Physically Handicapped in Springfield, Illinois and POWERHOUSE Energy Museum in Zion, Illinois. Tigerman taught at many universities across the United States. He was the director of the School of Architecture at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Tigerman was born in Chicago to a Jewish family. He was married three times. He had two children. He died of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) on June 3, 2019 in Chicago. He was 88.

Stanley Stair (October 1900 – April 2008) was the last British West Indies Regiment veteran. He joined in Jamaica in 1916. He dug trenches in France. He lied about his age. Of the group of friends he had enlisted with in Jamaica, he was the only one to survive the war. At the end of the war he was awarded the British War Medal and the Victory Medal. He died in Animal Hill, Lucea, Jamaica, in April 2008 at the age of 107.

Stanley Norman Cohen (February 17, 1935) is an American geneticist. He was the Kwoh-Ting Li Professor in the Stanford University School of Medicine. Cohen and Herbert Boyer were the first scientists to transplant genes from one living organism to another.

Stanley Rensch (18 April 1940 – 10 November 2024) was a Surinamese human rights activist. Born in Ganzee on 18 April 1940, Rensch moved to the Netherlands in 1960, where he studied pedagogy in Utrecht. After his studies, he returned to Suriname in 1973 and worked at the Ministry of Education and Community Development. His goal was to improve the education system in the run-up to the country's independence. After the 1980 Surinamese coup d'état and the subsequent 1982 December murders, Rensch became an outspoken critic of the military regime led by Desi Bouterse. In 1987, Rensch founded the human rights organization Moiwana '86, named after the 1986 Moiwana massacre during the Surinamese Interior War. With this organization, he documented human rights violations and offered support to victims and their families. Rensch died in the Surinam capital Paramaribo on 10 November 2024, at the age of 84.

Sir Stanley Spencer (30 June 1891 – 14 December 1959) was an English painter. He was inspired by the landscapes of his birthplace, Cookham, in Berkshire, a village near the River Thames, and also by his Christian faith, even not conventional. He created several Biblical inspired scenes set in his birthplace, with the villagers as their characters. An independent artist, he drew influences from several styles, including post-impressionism, realism and expressionism.

Stanton Terry Friedman (July 29, 1934 – May 13, 2019) was an American-Canadian nuclear physicist and professional ufologist He was the original civilian investigator of the Roswell incident. He worked on research and development projects for several large companies and tried to prove that aliens exist. Friedman was born in Elizabeth, New Jersey and moved to New Brunswick. Friedman died suddenly on May 13, 2019 while traveling from Toronto to Fredericton, New Brunswick at the age of 84. Flying Saucers & Science, June 2008, 320P. Captured! The Betty and Barney Hill UFO Experience. Co-author Kathleen Marden. Career Press / New Page Books, 2007., Top Secret/MAJIC, Marlowe + Co. 2005.. 296 pages, Crash at Corona: The Definitive Story of The Roswell Incident. Co-author Don Berliner, 1997. Science was Wrong: Startling truths about cures, theories, and inventions "They" declared impossible. Co-author Kathleen Marden. Pompton Plains, NJ: New Page Books. 2010.

Star Wars Outlaws is an new videogame of Star Wars, to the sequel is the Star Wars Outlaws 2 (2027), This new videogame was released for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and Series S and Microsoft Windows on August 30, 2024.

Publius Papinius Statius (about 45 – 96 A.D.) was a Roman poet born in Naples, Italy. Published in 92 A.D., his major epic was called Thebaid. It has the same theme as the Seven Against Thebes, a play by Aeschylus, the fight of seven city states against Thebes. He also wrote poems for different occasions. These poems are known as Silvae today. They show what the life at the court of Domitian was like. Even though he is not well-known today, he was better known during his time. He also appears in The Divine Comedy.

Stede Bonnet (c. 1688 – December 10, 1718) was an early 18th-century Barbadian pirate, sometimes called "the gentleman pirate" because he was a moderately rich landowner before turning to a life of crime. Bonnet was captured and was executed by hanging at White Point Garden, in Charleston, South Carolina on 10 December 1718.

Stedman Graham (born March 6, 1951) is an American businessperson, author, speaker and an educator. He is an African American who was born in Whitesboro, New Jersey. He is best known as Oprah Winfrey's partner.

A steering wheel is a circular object used by the driver of a car or boat to change the direction it is moving. The earliest known use of a steering wheel can be traced back to 1894 when Alfred Vacheron used one on his custom four-horsepower Panhard to participate in the Paris-Rouen race. That race in France in 1894 is one of the earliest known instances of a wheel-shaped device being used to steer a car. In 1898 the French manufacturer introduced a steering wheel in all its models. Other manufacturers followed suit – and the steering wheel became a set part of automotive design. Early on, carmakers also began installing bulb horns on steering wheels, for as traffic increased, it became necessary to warn other drivers as well as pedestrians and cyclists. For about two decades thereafter, steering wheels were incredibly simple: wooden circles directly connected to the wheel axis. They served no other task and could be extremely hard to turn, especially at low speeds or when stationary. Though power steering patents were circulating as early as the steering wheel itself, it was quite a long time before these systems were used. In the 1920s, an engineer named Francis W. Davis wanted to make truck driving a little easier and invented the first power steering system to be fitted into a vehicle, which was inspired by earlier work on power steering systems used in ships. In the 1950s it became popular to line steering wheels with real or artificial leather, which gave drivers a better grip.

Stefan Walter Hell (born 23 December 1962) is a German physicist. He is one of the directors of the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry in Göttingen, Germany. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2014 "for the development of super-resolved fluorescence microscopy", together with Eric Betzig and William Moerner. He was born into a Banat Swabian family in Arad, Romania, and grew up at his parents' home in nearby Sântana. In 1981, he began his studies at the Heidelberg University. He received his doctorate in physics in 1990.

Stefan Lorenz Radt (4 August 1927 − 22 November 2017) was a German-born Dutch historian of Jewish descent, author and academic who works in ancient Greek geography. He was born in Berlin, but was raised in The Hague. He was known for his books Tragicorum Graecorum Fragmenta, Strabons Geographika, and The Importance Of The Context. He fled to the Netherlands in 1937. Radt died in The Hague on 22 November 2017 at the age of 90.

Carl Stefan Erling Persson (; born 4 October 1947) is a Swedish businessman. In March 2013, Forbes reported Persson's net worth as $28 billion. making him the richest of Sweden's 12 billionaires and the 17th richest person in the world; Persson is the chairman and main shareholder in fashion company H&M, which was founded by his father Erling Persson in 1947.

Stefan Kapłaniak "Cenek" (10 April 1933 – 8 August 2021) was a Polish sprint canoer. He competed from the late 1950s to the mid-1960s. He competed in three Summer Olympics. He won a bronze medal at the 1960. Kapłaniak also won two gold medals at the 1958 ICF Canoe Sprint World Championships in Prague. He was born in Szczawnica, Poland. Kapłaniak died on 8 August 2021 in Chicago, Illinois at the age of 88.

Stefan Arczyński (31 July 1916 – 28 August 2022) was a Polish photographer and veteran of World War II. He worked in Essen, Berlin, and Wrocław. He took pictures for magazine covers and for postcards; he also photographed art. Arczyński died on 28 August 2022, at the age of 106.

Stefanie Zweig (19 September 1932 – 25 April 2014) was a German writer. She was best known for her autobiographical novel, Nirgendwo in Afrika (Nowhere in Africa, 1998), based on her early life in Kenya. The novel was made into a movie and won an Academy Award in 2002 for Best Foreign Language Film. Zweig was born in Leobschütz, Upper Silesia (now Poland). Her family was Jewish and fled Nazi Germany to Kenya. Zweig died after a short illness on 25 April 2014 in Frankfurt, Hesse, Germany. She was 81.

Stefania Jabłońska (born Szela Ginzburg; 7 September 1920 – 8 May 2017) was a Polish physician and professor, specializing in dermatology. She worked at the Medical University of Warsaw. In 1972, she theorized the association of human papilloma viruses with skin cancer in epidermodysplasia verruciformis. In 1978, Jabłońska and Gerard Orth at the Pasteur Institute discovered HPV-5 in skin cancer. Jabłońska was awarded the 1985 Robert Koch Prize. She was a recipient of the National Order of Merit and the Commander's Cross of the Order of Polonia Restituta.

Stefan Wyszyński (3 August 1901 – 28 May 1981) was a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who served as the Primate of Poland and Archbishop of Warsaw from 1948 until his death in 1981. He was made a Cardinal in 1953 and was beatified in 2021. Stefan Wyszyński was born in Zuzela, Poland. He was ordained a priest on 3 August 1924 by Bishop Wojciech Owczarek. Wyszyński was appointed the Bishop of Lublin in 1946 and consecrated by Cardinal August Hlond. In 1948, he became the Archbishop of Warsaw and Gniezno and was named the Primate of Poland. Pope Pius XII made him a cardinal in 1953. He played a significant role in opposing the communist regime in Poland. Stefan Wyszyński was beatified on 12 September 2021 by Pope Francis. The beatification ceremony at the Temple of Divine Providence was led by Cardinal Marcello Semeraro.

Stefania Burzmińska or Diamant (née Podgórska; between about 1921 and 1926 Sept. 29, 2018), was a Polish-born American woman who was awarded with the title of the Righteous Among the Nations in 1979 for hiding 13 Jews in her apartment during the German occupation of Poland from 1939 to 1945 during World War II. Stefania Burzmińska or Diamant (née Podgórska) was born between about 1921 and 1926, probably somewhere in Przemyśl County, Second Polish Republic (today located in Poland). Her father died in 1938 after suffering from a serious illness. In 1939, Stefania Podgórska started working in the city of Przemyśl in a shop which was owned by the Jewish Diamant family. Sometime during the German occupation of Poland from 1939 to 1945, Stefania Podgórska hid 13 Jews in the attic of her house. The 13 Jews that Stefania Podgórska hid and rescued were refugees fleeing and escaping from the German officers. All 13 of the Jews who were rescued and hidden by Podgórska survived the Holocaust and were ultimately liberated and freed by the Soviet Red Army. After their liberation, Stefania Podgórska married Max Diamant, who was one of the 13 Jews she hid in the attic of her house, and Stefania adopted her husband's surname Diamant after their marriage. In 1961, the couple Stefania and her husband Max Diamant ultimately left Poland and immigrated to the United States. While in the United States, Max Diamant changed his name to Józef Burzmiński, which is why Stefania Diamant changed her name to Stefania Burzmińska. Om January 11, 1979, Stefania Burzmińska was awarded with the title of the Righteous Among the Nations and was even given a medal for severely risking her life to save 13 Jews which she hid in her attic in German-occupied Poland during World War II, which was punishable by death. Stefania Burzmińska died on Sept. 29, 2018 in the city of Los Angeles, United States, aged somewhere between about 91 and 97 years old. Stefania Burzmińska was remembered for the efforts and humanitarian actions she undertook during World War II to save and rescue Jews at her funeral ceremony and burial.

Stefano Benni (12 August 1947 – 9 September 2025) was an Italian satirical writer, poet and journalist. His books were translated into around 20 foreign languages. He was born in Bologna, Italy. Benni died on 9 September 2025 in Bologna from problems caused by a stroke, aged 78. Terra, Pantheon Books, New York, 1985. Timeskipper, translator Antony Shugaar, Europa Editions, New York, 2008. Margherita Dolce Vita, translator Antony Shugaar, Europa Editions, New York, 2008. The story of Cyrano de Bergerac, Pushkin Children's Books, London, 2014.

Stefanía Fernández Krupij (born September 4, 1990) is a Venezuelan beauty pageant titleholder, humanitarian and political activist who participated in the 2014 Venezuela Protests, and was awarded Miss Venezuela 2008 as well as Miss Universe 2009 titles. Fernández is also the face of Avon Products, and was listed among the 50 Most Beautiful People list by People en Español. She has participated in many humanitarian activities, including fighting for AIDS awareness and fighting against human rights violations. Fernández also earned a Guinness record by becoming the first Miss Universe winner who was crowned by a compatriot. Fernández was born on Tuesday, September 4, 1990, in Mérida, Venezuela, to Nadia Krupij Holojad and José Luis Fernández. Fernández lives in Bogota, Colombia with her husband, Bernardo Ausaje, an investor, who she wedded in Colombia on May 6, 2017. Fernández has participated in political protest, and humane causes. During her time as Miss Universe, she traveled to many countries to spread AIDS awareness and participated in the 2014 Venezuela revolts. Fernández won the Miss Venezuela 2008 title in a pageant held in Caracas on September 10, 2008. She was crowned by the outgoing titleholder, Dayana Mendoza, Miss Venezuela 2007 and Miss Universe 2008. She was also awarded "Miss Elegance", "Best Body", and "Best Face" titles. She became the second Miss Trujillo to win that title since the Miss Venezuela pageant first began in 1952 and also the second Miss Trujillo to win Miss Universe. The first was Bárbara Palacios, Miss Venezuela 1986 and Miss Universe 1986. Miss Universe 2008, Dayana Mendoza (also from Venezuela) crowned her as Miss Universe 2009 on August 23, 2009, in Nassau, Bahamas. This marked the first time in Miss Universe history the same country won the crown two years in a row. Fernández was also recognized as among the 50 Most Beautiful People list by People en Español and in March 2010, Fernández officially became the face of Avon Products. Stefanía's husband was Bernardo Ausaje, an investor, who she wedded in Cartagena, Colombia, on May 6, 2017. In June 2020, however, Stefanía confirmed her decision to divorce Ausaje. Her manager, Luis Bascaran, released the following statement on social media:After three years of marriage, we want to inform you that by mutual agreement Bernardo and I have made the decision to separate (…) we have managed to make this decision from wisdom and maturity. We appreciate your respect and understanding. We will not be giving more statements on the subject. Fernández subsequently began a relationship with athlete Ender Inciarte, revealed in December 2020, and in May 2021, they had a son, named Liam. Fernández has traveled to several countries to spread awareness of AIDS. In November, 2010, she traveled again to Indonesia, specifically to the Bali island, when she filmed a commercial about vitamins. On her return to New York, she was in a press conference about HIV, in which she appeared with Ban Ki-moon, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, and with recognised Venezuelan fashion designer Carolina Herrera. On 5 November 2009, she served as a presenter at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, United States, sharing with Puerto Rican salsa singer Víctor Manuelle. At her second presentation in Venezuela, specifically in the Plaza de Toros Monumental de Maracaibo, where there was a crowd of 15,000 people, they gave a recognition (Orchid Award) to Fernández at Orchid Festival of Chinita Fair. She also traveled to Cannes, France, on 9 December 2009, for the Five Star Diamond awards, with Miss USA Kristen Dalton, and to Willemstad, Curaçao and Barquisimeto, Venezuela, as well, in early January 2010, for the Procesión de la Divina Pastora (Procession of the Holy Shepherdess). Fernández traveled to Puerto Rico in February 2010 to host Levántate, a Telemundo TV show; then travelled to New York, where she appeared on The Oprah Winfrey Show. In October 2010, Fernández traveled to Jakarta, Bandung and Medan, in Indonesia, where she crowned the Indonesian representative for the Miss Universe 2010 pageant. In September, March, and April 2010, she travelled to Moscow, Russia; São Paulo, Brazil; Mumbai, India; Nassau, Bahama; Caracas, Venezuela; and Prague, Czech Republic, where she crowned the respective representatives of those countries for the Miss Universe 2010 pageant. She then flew to Colombia (she was invited to promote the Kimberly-Clark brand), Panama (where she served as a presenter for Sony), and to Puerto Rico again, for the Puerto Rico Open. Stefanía promised to spend her year-long reign as Miss Universe traveling the world raising awareness on humanitarian issues and promoting education regarding HIV/AIDS. During her reign, Stefanía traveled to Indonesia, Curaçao, France, Puerto Rico, Russia, Colombia, Panama, the Czech Republic, the Bahamas, Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Brazil, India, Spain, Rwanda, Venezuela, Argentina, and Ecuador for an AIDS awareness tour In 2010. Hugo Chávez, president of Venezuela, thanked her, giving her the support of both him and his government for this act. On August 23, 2010, Stefanía, still just a teenager, passed her crown to Ximena Navarrete (Miss Mexico). During her final catwalk, she opened a flag of Venezuela with only seven stars. The Venezuelan parliament (the National Assembly) had voted a modification of the flag from seven to eight stars in 2006; former President Chávez had favored this decision. The display of the old flag was seen by Investor's Business Daily as a protest against the new policies of Chávez. During the 2014 Venezuelan protests, Stefanía participated in the "Your Voice is Your Power" campaign, fighting against violence, human rights violations and the censorship of media in Venezuela. Currently, Fernández also runs a successful beauty line, AMMATERRE, for vegan skin care products. 2009: Guinness record (for being the first Miss Universe winner who was crowned by a fellow member of her country). Stefanía is the face of Avon Products. She was listed among the 50 Most Beautiful People list by People en Español, a Spanish-language magazine.

Stefano Farina (19 September 1962 – 23 May 2017) was an Italian football referee. He was born in Ovada, Italy. Farina has refereed several high-profile matches in Serie A and the UEFA Champions League, including the 2006 UEFA Super Cup in Monaco. Farina officiated in qualifiers for the 2004 and 2008 European Championships, as well as preliminary matches for the 2002 and 2006 World Cups. He was known to have served as a FIFA referee during the period from 2001 to 2007. He retired internationally in 2007 after reaching the mandatory retirement age of 45. Farina died suddenly in Genova, Italy on 23 May 2017 from a suspected heart attack, aged 54.

Stefano Delle Chiaie (13 September 1936 – 10 September 2019) was an Italian neofascist activist. He was the founder of Avanguardia Nazionale, a member of Ordine Nuovo, and founder of Lega nazionalpopolare. He was a friend of Licio Gelli, grandmaster of P2 masonic lodge. He was suspected of involvement in South America's Operation Condor, but was acquitted. Delle Chiaie died on 10 September 2019 at a Rome hospital at the age of 82.

Stefon Marsean Diggs (born November 29, 1993) is an American football wide receiver for the Buffalo Bills of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football at Maryland. He was drafted by the Minnesota Vikings in the fifth round of the 2015 NFL Draft.

Steina Vasulka (born Steinunn Briem Bjarnadottir in 1940) and Woody Vasulka (born Bohuslav Vasulka on 20 January 1937 – 20 December 2019) are early known figures of video art. They are known for producing work since the early 1960s. The couple met in the early 1960s and moved to New York City in 1965, where they began showing video art at the Whitney Museum and founded The Kitchen in 1971. Steina and Woody both became Guggenheim fellows: Steina in 1976, and Woody in 1979. Woody died on 20 December 2019 in Santa Fe, New Mexico at the age of 82.

Stein Erik Hagen (22 July 1956 – 4 May 2026) was a Norwegian businessman. He is chairman of Orkla. Hagen holds large stakes in the companies Steen & Strøm, Jernia and Komplett. According to the magazine Kapital, Hagen has NOK 24 billion. It is making him the second richest person in Norway. Stein Erik Hagen was born 22 July 1956. He studied Kjøpmannsinsituttet. Together with his father he founded discount store chain called RIMI in the 1970s. In the 2000s he sold RIMI to Swedish companies ICA and Ahold. Most of the money he invested in the Orkla. At various times he financially supported different parties (Liberal Party, Christian Democratic Party, Conservative Party and Progress Party).

Stella Maris Turk, MBE (1925 – 3 April 2017) was a British zoologist, naturalist, and conservationist. Turk was known for her activities in marine biology and conservation as it applies to marine molluscs and mammals. Turk became a Member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire in 2002, and was awarded the Stamford Raffles Award by the Zoological Society of London in 1979.

Sten Lundin (20 November 1931 – 3 June 2016) was a Swedish professional motocross racer. He won the F.I.M. 500cc Motocross World Championship in 1959 riding a Monark. In the 1960 world championship, he finished in second place, two points behind Bill Nilsson. Lundin was also a member of the victorious Swedish team at the 1955 Motocross des Nations.

Stendhal (; 23 January 1783 – 23 March 1842) was the pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle, a French writer. He is best known for two novels. The first is Le Rouge et le Noir (The Red and the Black, 1830). The second is La Chartreuse de Parme (The Charterhouse of Parma, 1839). He also wrote books about love, art, music and travel. Several of his books tell the story of his own life. He was born in Grenoble, and he died in Paris. Stendhal had an unhappy childhood. His mother died when he was seven, and he did not love his father. As a young man, he followed the armies of Napoleon as an official. He went to Italy in 1800, and then to Germany and Austria. In 1812, he went to Russia with the French army. After the fall of Napoleon in 1814, he went to live in Milan. Italy became the country of his heart. From 1821 to 1830, he lived in Paris. There he was known as a witty talker in the salons, the social gatherings of the time. In 1831, he became the French consul in Civitavecchia. A consul is an official who represents his country in a foreign town. Civitavecchia was a small port in the lands of the Pope. He died in Paris in 1842, after a stroke, a sudden illness of the brain. He first became known for books on painting, music and travel. These early books drew heavily on the work of earlier writers, often without saying so. He signed them with false names. In 1817, he used the name Stendhal for the first time. His book De l'amour (On Love, 1822) explains how love grows in the mind. He called this process "crystallisation". In Racine et Shakespeare (1823), he defended a modern literature. He wrote his first novel, Armance, only at the age of forty-three. The Red and the Black tells the story of Julien Sorel. Julien is a poor and ambitious young man in France after the fall of Napoleon. Stendhal composed The Charterhouse of Parma in less than two months. He worked from drafts and dictated the text to a copyist. Its chapters on the Battle of Waterloo were admired by Balzac and later by Tolstoy. Many of his works stayed unfinished. Among them are the novels Lucien Leuwen and Lamiel. Another is the story of his childhood, Vie de Henry Brulard. They were published only many years after his death. Stendhal wanted a clear and simple style. He later claimed that he read the French Civil Code, the book of French civil law, to find the right tone. He often told his stories through the eyes of one character. At the same time, the narrator often speaks with humour and irony. The narrator is the voice that tells the story. His heroes are young people full of energy. They look for happiness in a society that blocks their way. He wrote for a few readers who could feel as he did. He called them "the happy few". His novels had only limited and uneven success during his life. But Balzac praised The Charterhouse of Parma in a long article. Stendhal believed that readers would understand him around 1880. At the end of the 19th century, he became one of the most loved writers in France. Today he is seen as one of the great novelists of the 19th century. Writers such as Tolstoy and Friedrich Nietzsche admired him. Much of what is known about Stendhal's childhood comes from his own account, the Life of Henry Brulard, which he wrote in 1835 and 1836. This book is not always exact. Michael Wood shows that its opening scene is a fiction. Victor Brombert shows that it hides as much as it shows: Stendhal wanted to be sincere, but he also enjoyed disguise. Many of the stories below are his own memories, told many years later. Marie-Henri Beyle was born on 23 January 1783 in Grenoble. The house stood in a narrow street, then called rue des Vieux-Jésuites. Today it is number 14, rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau. Henri was the oldest of three children and the only son. His sister Pauline was born in 1786, and his sister Zénaïde in 1788. His father, Chérubin Beyle, was a lawyer at the parliament of Grenoble. In France before the Revolution, a parliament was a high court of law. In his memories, Henri described his father as a cold man who thought all the time about buying and selling land. His mother, Henriette Gagnon, died in childbirth on 23 November 1790. She was thirty-three years old. Henri was seven. Much later, in his autobiography, the story of his own life, he described his love for her as a great passion. He wrote about it very openly. He also wrote that his inner life, the life of his mind and feelings, began with her death. He later remembered that at first he could not cry. He cried for her only more than a year later, alone in his bed at night. He began his autobiography on 23 November 1835. This was forty-five years to the day after her death. After this loss, the family lived a closed and quiet life. His mother's sister, Séraphie Gagnon, was very religious. In his memories, the boy saw her as an enemy. From December 1792, a priest called Raillane was his private teacher. He later wrote that he hated him. As he told it later, the adults kept him away from other children. He was not allowed to play in the street. He was not allowed to swim in the river Isère either. Raillane always spoke about the dangers of swimming, and Henri never learned to swim. His sister Pauline was his friend. His younger sister Zénaïde often told the adults what he did. In his account, his best refuge was his grandfather, Henri Gagnon. He was a respected doctor in Grenoble. He was also a man of the Enlightenment. This was the movement of the 18th century that trusted reason and science. His large house on the place Grenette was only about a hundred steps from the Beyle house. On its sunny terrace, the doctor taught the boy the names of the stars and of plants. The grandfather spoke Italian. The boy came to believe that the Gagnon family had come from Italy. In his mind, the Beyle side of the family meant power, money and coldness. The Gagnon side meant culture, wit, gaiety and tenderness. He connected this happy side with Italy. His great-aunt Élisabeth Gagnon and his uncle Romain Gagnon belonged to this side too. Romain was a lawyer who liked women. He took the boy to the theatre. Books gave him another way to escape. He talked about many of them with his grandfather. Among them were the French writers Fénelon and Molière, and the Latin poets Horace and Ovid. His mother had read Dante in Italian. Henri wrote his name for the first known time in her copy of the Divine Comedy. The long Italian poems of Ariosto and Tasso gave him a lasting love of passionate adventure stories. He also read La Nouvelle Héloïse, a novel by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in secret. In the family's country house at Claix, he read Don Quixote. He later remembered that the book made him laugh for the first time since his mother's death. His father, he wrote, tried several times to take it away from him. Henri grew up during the French Revolution. On 7 June 1788, the people of Grenoble rose against the king's soldiers. They threw tiles from the roofs. The event became known as the Day of the Tiles. The boy was five years old. He later remembered seeing a wounded worker slowly climb the stairs of the house next door. His family supported the king, but Henri became a passionate republican. King Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793. His family was in despair. He later wrote that he secretly felt great joy. On 26 April 1793, the revolutionary authorities in Grenoble published lists of people suspected of being against the Republic. His father's name was on the list of the "notoriously suspect". Goldzink writes that his father was held until July 1794. In the spring of 1794, Henri wrote a false letter to join the Battalion of Hope. This was a group of children organised by the Jacobins, the most active revolutionaries. His family discovered the trick. On 21 November 1796, Henri entered the École centrale of Grenoble. The Revolution had created such state schools to replace the old religious schools. For the first time, he had friends of his own age. Two of them were Félix Faure and Louis Crozet. His teacher of literature, Dubois-Fontanelle, showed him the great foreign writers. One of them was Shakespeare. He also learned drawing and logic. In these years he discovered music. He later called it his strongest and most costly passion. His aunt Séraphie died in 1797. Mathematics became his way out of Grenoble. Good students in mathematics could enter the new École Polytechnique, a school for engineers in Paris. Henri took private lessons from Gabriel Gros, a teacher who did not work at the school. Much later, the name Gros appeared again in The Red and the Black. On 15 September 1799, Henri won the first prize in mathematics. On 30 October, he left Grenoble for Paris. He later remembered that his father cried when he left. On 9 November 1799, he stopped at the coach station of Nemours. There he heard the news of a coup d'état. A coup d'état is a sudden and illegal seizure of power. General Bonaparte had taken control of the French government. Henri arrived in Paris the next day. He then changed his plans. He did not take the entrance examination of the École Polytechnique. Paris disappointed him. He felt very lonely, and he soon fell ill. His relatives, the Daru family, took care of him. Noël Daru, the head of the family, was a first cousin of his grandfather. In January 1800, his cousin Pierre Daru gave him a job at the Ministry of War. Pierre Daru was a powerful official. He was a hard and demanding master. He always thought that his young cousin knew nothing. On 7 May 1800, Henri left Paris to join Pierre Daru and his brother Martial, who were with the army on its way to Italy. On the way, a captain named Burelvillers taught him how to ride a horse. He also taught him how to use a sword. Henri crossed the Alps by the Great St Bernard Pass. At the top of the pass stood a hospice, a house where monks received travellers. He arrived there wet, tired and hungry. On the way to Milan, he heard an opera by Domenico Cimarosa. It was Il matrimonio segreto (The Secret Marriage). He felt a pure and perfect happiness. He never forgot it. Later, he often called himself "Dominique" in his private writings. The name came from the first name of Cimarosa. He reached Milan on 10 June 1800. There he met Angela Pietragrua, a beautiful married woman. He loved her in silence. He did not dare to tell her. On 23 September 1800, he became a second lieutenant in the 6th regiment of dragoons. He owed this post to Pierre Daru. Dragoons were soldiers who fought on horseback. He later used this experience of army life in his novel Lucien Leuwen. In 1801, General Michaud took him on his staff as an aide-de-camp, an officer who helps a general in his work. But the army bored him. In December 1801, he went back to France because he was ill. In a letter of 20 July 1802, he resigned from the army. He wanted to become a poet. From 1802 to 1806, Henri lived mostly in Paris. His father sent him money every month, first 150 francs and then 200 francs. It was enough to live on. It was not enough to dress in fashion. He wanted to become a great writer for the theatre. He started many plays. For years he worked on a comedy called Letellier, but he never finished it. In the opinion of Jean Goldzink, he had chosen the wrong form. He expected everything from the theatre. He came to the novel only in 1827. He read a great deal. He studied philosophers such as Hobbes, Condillac, Helvétius and Destutt de Tracy. Again and again, he read the plays of Shakespeare, Corneille and Molière. He also read those of the Italian poet Alfieri. His teachers in thought were the Idéologues. They were a group of thinkers who studied how the mind forms ideas. For Beyle, reading, writing and living were closely joined. He used books to understand himself and other people. He also kept a diary, his Journal. The part that survives begins on 18 April 1801. In these years, he worked out a personal method for finding happiness. It is known as "beylism", from his family name. Its aim was to know society and to know oneself. A person cannot change the world. But a person can change himself, and so take as much pleasure from life as possible. In long letters, he tried to teach these ideas to his sister Pauline. At this time, he did not admire Napoleon. He was a republican. In his diary, he attacked the union of religion and tyranny. His great admiration for the Emperor came only later. In December 1804, he met a young actress, Mélanie Guilbert, in a class for actors. Her stage name was Louason. She was one of only two women with whom he ever lived as a couple. In 1805, she went to work at the theatre of Marseille, and he followed her. In Marseille, he worked for a business that exported goods. In Marseille, he also wanted to start a bank. But his father refused to give him the money. So he worked for a trading house and kept its accounts, from July 1805 to May 1806. Mélanie left Marseille on 1 March 1806. By then, Henri had failed in love, in literature and in business. On 16 October 1806, Henri followed Martial Daru to Germany. On 27 October, he entered Berlin behind Napoleon's army, which had just defeated the Prussians. Two days later, he became an assistant to the war commissioners. These were the officials who supplied the army. On 8 November, he left with Martial Daru for the city of Brunswick. He worked hard, but he was often bored. He fell in love with Wilhelmine von Griesheim, the daughter of the former governor of Brunswick. He called her Mina. He left Brunswick in November 1808. In 1809, he followed Pierre Daru in the war against Austria. He was not present at the great Battle of Wagram. But his work was to find lodgings and hospitals for the army. So he saw the war from close behind the front line. According to Goldzink, this experience helped him later. It helped him to describe the Battle of Waterloo in The Charterhouse of Parma. A decree of 1 August 1810 made him an auditor at the Council of State. Auditors were young officials who helped this high council of the government in its work. He was also made an inspector of the furniture and buildings of the Crown. He worked on the lists of the Musée Napoléon, today the Louvre. This work opened the history of art to him. Now he lived like a rich young man. He wrote his name "de Beyle", as if he were a noble. He had a carriage, fine clothes and debts. His mistress, Angelina Bereyter, was a singer. She sang the music of Cimarosa and Mozart for him. In secret, he loved Alexandrine Daru, the wife of Pierre Daru. On 29 August 1811, he left for Italy. He felt that he needed to love and to be loved. In Milan, he knocked at the door of Angela Pietragrua, eleven years after their first meeting. She recognised him and cried out that he was "the Chinese man". On 21 September 1811, she finally became his lover. He wrote the date and the hour on his braces. During this journey, he had the idea of a book on the history of Italian painting. On 23 July 1812, he left Paris in a carriage. He was going to follow the Grande Armée, Napoleon's great army, into Russia, as a messenger of the Emperor. He carried official letters, the unfinished Letellier, and the manuscript of his book on Italian painting. He saw the city of Smolensk in flames. Then he saw the great fire of Moscow in September 1812. In Moscow, he took only one book, a volume of Voltaire. During the terrible retreat, the army suffered from hunger, cold and the attacks of the Cossacks. Beyle kept his calm. He even took time to shave in freezing weather. He crossed the bridges of the Berezina River early, before the great crowd arrived. The manuscript on painting was lost on the way. Only Letellier came back. He was back in Paris on 31 January 1813. In April, he was sent to Germany again, where the war had started once more. On 20 May 1813, he watched the Battle of Bautzen. He wrote that all one can see of a battle is nothing. But illness sent him home. He spent the autumn of 1813 in Milan. In December 1813, he was named assistant to Count de Saint-Vallier. The count had to organise the defence of Grenoble against the allied armies. At the end of March 1814, he returned to Paris. On 30 March, the armies fought on the hill of Montmartre, at the edge of the city. These events left him indifferent. He saw the fall of Napoleon and the return of the Bourbon kings. The new government ended the post of auditor, and Beyle lost his position. He later wrote that the fall of the Empire had given him pleasure. He sold everything and decided to live in Italy, where life cost half as much. In the spring and early summer of 1814, he wrote his first book. It was called Vies de Haydn, de Mozart et de Métastase (Lives of Haydn, Mozart and Metastasio). Much of it was copied from other authors. He left Paris on 20 July. He reached Milan on 10 August 1814. He lived in Milan until 1821, with some long journeys. His love for Angela Pietragrua did not bring him happiness. She kept him at a distance and sent him away on journeys. On 15 October 1815, he wrote in his diary that his love was dead. In December 1815, she ended the relationship. Later, his friend Prosper Mérimée told a story about this break. Stendhal, he said, had seen Angela with another man through a hole in a door. Goldzink doubts this story. He thinks that it belongs to the image of himself that Stendhal liked to give to others. In these years, he signed his books with false names. His first book was signed Louis-Alexandre-César Bombet. The next one was signed M.B.A.A. The letters meant "Monsieur Beyle, Ancien Auditeur" (Mr Beyle, former auditor). This was the Histoire de la peinture en Italie (History of Painting in Italy, 1817). Again, Beyle copied large parts of it from other books. The same year, Rome, Naples et Florence en 1817 (Rome, Naples and Florence in 1817) appeared. It was signed "M. de Stendhal, cavalry officer". This was the first time that the name Stendhal appeared. The name comes from Stendal, a small town in Prussia, on the road from Hanover to Berlin. Beyle had probably passed through it in 1806. He added an "h" to the name. Stendal was also the birthplace of the art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann. Some writers think that this is why he chose it. Milan was the city of his heart. Every evening, he went to the opera house La Scala. He stayed there from seven o'clock until midnight. The private boxes of La Scala were like drawing rooms, where people met and talked. On 15 October 1816, at La Scala, he met the English poet Lord Byron. They met in the box of his friend Ludovico di Breme. He told Byron amazing stories about Napoleon. Many of them were not true. Between 1814 and 1821, he spent about two years away from Milan. He travelled in Italy, went back to France, and visited England in 1817. During a stay in Paris in 1817, he met Destutt de Tracy, whose books he had admired for twelve years. The philosopher came to see him at his hotel. Stendhal admired him so much that he could hardly talk to him. In Milan, he also took part in the debates about Romanticism. This was a new movement in literature and the arts. He wrote three short essays on these questions, but they were not published at the time. He later used these ideas in his book Racine et Shakespeare. On 4 March 1818, he met Matilde Dembowski. He always called her Métilde. She was twenty-eight. She lived apart from her husband, a violent Polish general. Stendhal loved her with a passion that made him shy and clumsy. She never returned his love. She was also close to the Carbonari. These were secret groups that fought against Austrian rule in Italy. In June 1819, he followed her in secret to the small town of Volterra, where her two sons were at school. He wore green glasses so that she would not recognise him. But she saw him at once, and she was angry. From this unhappy love came his book De l'amour (On Love). He found its main idea on 29 December 1819. He called this day his "day of genius". He finished the book in March 1820. His father died in Grenoble on 20 June 1819 and left him almost nothing. The Austrian police now arrested many patriots among the friends of Métilde. People advised Stendhal to go back to France. He left Milan on 13 June 1821. In his own words, Milan remained for him "the flower of his life". Stendhal reached Paris on 21 June 1821. He hid his pain from his friends. In his memoir Souvenirs d'égotisme, he wrote that his only idea was "not to be guessed". So he wore a mask. In company, he became a witty, provocative and cynical talker. He liked to shock people with his words. According to F. W. J. Hemmings, people began at this time to see him as a brilliant talker, and also a dangerous one. He spent his evenings in the salons of Paris. On Saturdays, he went to the scientist Georges Cuvier. On Sundays, he went to the philosopher Destutt de Tracy. On Tuesdays, he went to Madame Ancelot. Destutt de Tracy was the founder of "Ideology". He had been Stendhal's master in thought since his youth. From February 1822, he also went to the attic room of the critic Étienne-Jean Delécluze. He went there on Sunday afternoons. Young writers met there to talk and to argue. He needed money. On 1 November 1822, he began to write for an English magazine, the New Monthly Magazine. Later he also wrote for the London Magazine and others. He wrote them in French, and they were translated into English. For the New Monthly Magazine alone, he received about 200 pounds a year. From 1824, he also wrote about art and music for a Paris newspaper, the Journal de Paris. In 1824, he wrote seventeen articles on the great art exhibition of that year, the Salon. Between 1822 and 1829, he published more than a hundred articles. He visited England in 1821, and again in 1826. In London, he saw the actor Edmund Kean play Shakespeare's Othello. His books of these years made his name known. De l'amour appeared in August 1822, but it had no success. His Vie de Rossini (Life of Rossini, 1823) was his first real success. The same year, he published Racine et Shakespeare. This short book argued for a modern literature. The first edition had only three hundred copies. A second part followed in 1825. That year, Métilde Dembowski died in Milan. In 1824, he began a love affair with Clémentine Curial, a married countess. It lasted about two years. Later, his cousin Romain Colomb destroyed her many letters to him. Stendhal came back from England in 1826. He then found that she had a new lover. He suffered greatly. In 1826, at the age of forty-three, he wrote his first novel, Armance. It appeared in August 1827, and it failed. From 1827, his income from journalism fell. He had serious money problems. On 1 January 1828, he arrived in Milan. The Austrian police gave him twelve hours to leave. The reason was his book Rome, Naples et Florence, which had appeared again in 1827. In 1829, he published Promenades dans Rome (Walks in Rome), a guide to the city. He also published a short story, Vanina Vanini. The same year, he had a short affair with Alberthe de Rubempré. She was a cousin of the painter Eugène Delacroix. During a journey in the south of France, he had the idea for a new novel. It came to him in Marseille, on the night of 25–26 October 1829. The novel became Le Rouge et le Noir (The Red and the Black). In February 1830, a young Italian woman, Giulia Rinieri, told him that she loved him. She knew, she said, that he was old and ugly. She became his lover on 22 March 1830. She was born in Siena in 1801, and she lived in Paris in the house of her guardian, the Tuscan minister Berlinghieri. Then came the July Revolution of 1830. King Charles X lost his throne. Louis-Philippe became king of the French. Stendhal watched the fighting from Giulia's home. He asked to be made a prefect, the head of the government in a French department. But he did not get the post. On 25 September 1830, he was made a consul instead. He asked to marry Giulia, but her guardian refused. On 6 November 1830, Stendhal left Paris for Trieste. The Red and the Black appeared on 13 November, after he had gone. Stendhal arrived in Trieste on 25 November 1830. But Trieste belonged to the Austrian Empire. In December, the Austrian government refused to accept him. It saw him as a dangerous liberal, who had already been sent out of Milan. The Austrian chancellor, Metternich, refused to accept him as consul. Stendhal was sent instead to Civitavecchia. This was a port of the Papal States, on the Mediterranean Sea. The Papal States were the lands ruled by the Pope in central Italy. He began work there on 17 April 1831. Civitavecchia was a small and dirty town of about 7,500 people. A thousand convicts also lived there, in chains. The town lay about eighty kilometres from Rome. His pay fell from 15,000 to 10,000 francs a year. He was bored and lonely. He went to Rome as often as he could. Goldzink has counted his absences. In eleven years, he was away from Civitavecchia for about four and a half years. His best friend in the town was Donato Bucci, who sold antiques. Bucci later received Stendhal's library. In 1835, Stendhal finally received the cross of the Legion of Honour. He had asked for it for a long time. In February 1831, he decided not to publish anything while he worked for the government. But he did not stop writing. From 20 June to 4 July 1832, he wrote Souvenirs d'égotisme (Memoirs of an Egotist). It tells the story of his years in Paris. In May 1834, he began a new novel, Lucien Leuwen. In November 1835, he put it aside. He began to write the story of his childhood, the Vie de Henry Brulard (The Life of Henry Brulard). All these works stayed unfinished. None of them appeared during his life. Giulia Rinieri married another man in June 1833. They remained friends. In December of that year, he went back to Italy. On a steamboat going down the river Rhône, he met the writers George Sand and Alfred de Musset by chance. They travelled together as far as Marseille. His eyes became weak. From 1 September 1835, he wore glasses. He also began to dictate his texts to a copyist. On 26 March 1836, he learned that he could go to Paris on leave. He stopped writing Henry Brulard at once. He had a protector, Count Molé. Molé was the head of the French government from 1836 to 1839. Thanks to him, the leave became longer and longer. Stendhal stayed away from his post for three years, from May 1836 to August 1839. He was still paid. He travelled across France. He also went to Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium. From these journeys came the Mémoires d'un touriste (Memoirs of a Tourist), published in June 1838. In 1833, in Rome, he had found some old Italian manuscripts in family archives. He now made stories from them. Most of them appeared in the Revue des Deux Mondes, a Paris magazine, between 1837 and 1839. On 16 August 1838, he thought of making a short novel from one of these old Italian stories. In September, he decided to move the action to the 19th century. On 4 November 1838, he shut himself up in his flat in the rue Caumartin, in Paris. On 26 December, he gave his cousin Romain Colomb six large notebooks: the novel was finished. The main writing had taken him less than eight weeks. He signed a contract with the publisher on 24 January 1839. On 17 March 1839, the newspaper Le Constitutionnel printed the episode of Waterloo in advance. On 6 April 1839, the official list of new books, the Bibliographie de la France, announced La Chartreuse de Parme (The Charterhouse of Parma). Stendhal had sold it for 2,500 francs. In December 1839, a volume of his Italian stories followed. It took its title from the longest of them, L'Abbesse de Castro. It was the last book that Stendhal published during his life. On 13 April 1839, he began a very different novel, Lamiel. He never managed to finish it. Count Molé lost power in March 1839. Stendhal had to leave Paris on 24 June. He went back to his post at Civitavecchia in August 1839. On 25 September 1840, Honoré de Balzac published a long article on The Charterhouse of Parma. It appeared in his own magazine, the Revue parisienne. Stendhal read it in Civitavecchia in the middle of October 1840. He then began to correct his novel, as Balzac had advised. Balzac had already praised the novel in April 1839. In a letter to Madame Hanska, he called it the finest book published in fifty years. In eighteen months, the public bought the 1,200 copies of the first edition. His health became worse. On 1 January 1840, he fainted while he was correcting Lamiel, and he fell into the fire. On 15 March 1841, he had a stroke. He wrote that he had "fought with nothingness". In October 1841, he was given leave because of his health. He left for Paris on 21 October. There he seemed to recover. On 21 March 1842, he signed an agreement to write stories for the Revue des Deux Mondes. In his last months, he was working on an Italian story, Suora Scolastica. On the next day, 22 March 1842, in the early evening, he fell down at the corner of the rue Neuve-des-Capucines. He had had another stroke. He died on 23 March at two in the morning, without waking up. He was fifty-nine years old. He was buried in the Montmartre Cemetery on 24 March. Some time before, he had written a joke in a letter to his friend Fiore. There was nothing ridiculous, he wrote, about dying in the street. But one should not do it on purpose. Stendhal had wished to be buried at Andilly, a village near Montmorency, north of Paris. In his will, he added that the Montmartre Cemetery would do if Andilly cost too much. He was buried at Montmartre. In Souvenirs d'égotisme, Stendhal had written his own epitaph, the words for his grave. He wrote it in Italian: "Errico Beyle, Milanese. Visse, scrisse, amò" ("Henri Beyle, of Milan. He lived, wrote, loved"). A second line said that his soul loved Cimarosa, Mozart and Shakespeare. The stone on his grave changed the order of the words. It reads "Scrisse, amò, visse" (wrote, loved, lived). It also left out the names of the three artists, and it gives his first name as "Arrigo" instead of "Errico". During his life, Stendhal published three finished novels. They were Armance (1827), The Red and the Black (1830) and The Charterhouse of Parma (1839). He also published some short stories. Most of them take place in Italy in the time of the Renaissance. But a large part of his work was found in his papers after his death. Hemmings writes about his fame as a novelist today. In his view, it rests almost as much on these unfinished works as on his published books. The first editions of these papers were often faulty and incomplete. Stendhal first became known for books about art, music and travel. His first book, the lives of Haydn, Mozart and Metastasio, was signed with the false name Bombet. Goldzink calls it an undeniable plagiarism: much of it was taken from other writers. With this book began one of his favourite kinds of writing, the life of an artist. He paid for the printing himself. A thousand copies were printed, but only a little more than a hundred were sold. The History of Painting in Italy (1817) was also largely taken from others. Alter and Cosman note that more than two thirds of it was compiled from writers such as Lanzi, Reynolds and Vasari. But at that time, authors of such compilations did not have to give references, and Stendhal knew that he was using sources. But Goldzink finds in it some of the central themes of his work. Art, history and politics meet there, all under the sign of Italy. The book reaches its highest point with Michelangelo and Raphael. With Rome, Naples and Florence in 1817, Beyle found his pen name. He also found one of his favourite forms, the travel diary. And he found his own way of mixing tourism, the arts, the manners of a people and politics. A new and much changed version of the book appeared in 1827. His first success came from music, and therefore from Italy. It was the Life of Rossini (1823), a book about the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini. Walks in Rome (1829) looks like a tourist guide written as a diary. For generations, travellers took it with them to Rome. Goldzink sees in it much more than a guide. For him, it is the most convenient way to travel inside Stendhal's mind. Stendhal gave his readers some advice. They should cross out each short article with a pencil. They should do it as soon as they had seen the monument. In the Memoirs of a Tourist (1838), the narrator pretends to be a travelling salesman of iron goods. He journeys through France. Goldzink notes that Stendhal helped to bring two English words into French. They were égotisme (egotism, the habit of talking and writing about oneself) and tourisme (tourism). For Michel Crouzet, the Italy of these books is not only a real country. It is also a "myth", a set of desires for which Italy serves as a mirror. In this sense, Italy belongs to Stendhal's own work. He wrote it as much as he described it. De l'amour (On Love, 1822) was born from his unhappy passion for Métilde Dembowski. Goldzink calls it a confession dressed up as a treatise, a serious study of love. In fact, it deals mostly with passionate love. The book shows how close love and art are to each other. In this way, Goldzink writes, it gives a key to all of Stendhal's work. It is one of his least read books. But some critics see it as the secret centre of his work. The book describes the birth of love step by step. First comes admiration. Then a person imagines the pleasure of kissing the loved one. Hope follows, and then love is born. After that comes "crystallisation", the most famous idea of the book. Stendhal took the word from the salt mines of Salzburg. Workers threw a bare branch into the deep parts of the mine. Two or three months later, they took it out. It was covered with shining crystals, like diamonds. In the same way, the mind of a lover finds new perfections in the loved person. It finds them in everything around it. Later comes doubt. Then a "second crystallisation" adds the certainty of being loved in return. Stendhal also divided love into four kinds. The first is passionate love, like the love of Héloïse for Abélard. The second is love as a matter of taste, the kind that was common in Paris. The third is physical love. The fourth is love from vanity, when a man wants to be admired for winning a woman. Dominique Fernandez points out that Stendhal mixed these serious classes with comments that make fun of them. The book had no success at all when it appeared. According to a story told later, the publisher sold the unsold copies as ballast for a ship. Racine et Shakespeare (1823 and 1825) is a short polemical book. Such a book is written to attack some ideas and to defend others. It defends a modern, energetic and original literature. Stendhal had developed its ideas in Milan. According to Goldzink, he turned the Italian word romanticismo into a French word, romanticisme. He is also often credited with making the word romantisme known in France. In Milan, he had already planned essays called "What is romanticism?" and "On romanticism in the fine arts". His definition was simple. Romantic art gives people the works that bring them the most pleasure. It takes into account their present habits and beliefs. Classic art gives them the works that pleased their great-grandfathers. In this sense, he wrote, the Greek poets Sophocles and Euripides had been romantic in their own time. So had the French poet Racine. For the theatre, this meant historical and national plays written in prose, not in verse. The second part of the book (1825) answered an attack on Romanticism. The attack came from Auger, a member of the Académie française. Yet Stendhal did not fit easily into the Romantic school of his time. Romantic plays bored him, and he disliked their grand verse. He could not bear the "infamous rhetoric" of the followers of Chateaubriand. Goldzink calls him a son of the Enlightenment and a child of the Revolution. Still, some people of his time saw him as a leader of the new movement. He himself said that he had thrown himself into the quarrel of the Romantics. Michel Crouzet adds that Stendhal found in these debates a theory of art based on energy and strong emotion. In the language of the 18th century, this was called the "sublime". In 1825, Stendhal also published a short pamphlet, D'un nouveau complot contre les industriels (On a New Plot against the Industrialists). In it, he attacked people in his own liberal camp. They saw the owners of industry as the saviours of humanity. Armance (1827) was Stendhal's first novel. Its subtitle is "Some scenes from a Paris salon in 1827". According to Yves Ansel, the publisher, Urbain Canel, chose this subtitle to help the book sell. The story began with a rumour. In 1825, people said that a fashionable writer, the Duchess of Duras, had written a new novel. Its hero, they said, was impotent: he could not have sexual relations. Another writer, Henri de Latouche, quickly wrote an imitation of it as a literary joke. In those works, the impotent hero was called Olivier. Stendhal first thought of using this name too. He then chose Octave, and he gave the title of the book to the young woman, Armance. The hero of Armance is Octave de Malivert, a young nobleman with republican ideas. He has become rich through a new law. This law paid back nobles for the lands they had lost during the Revolution. He has sworn never to love. But he falls in love with his cousin, Armance de Zohiloff. She is an orphan girl who lives with a relative. Octave marries Armance. Then he kills himself, and he leaves her a letter. He takes poison on a ship near the coast of Greece. Armance and his mother then enter a convent. The novel never says clearly what Octave's secret is. The reader has to guess his impotence. Goldzink suggests that the secret also works as an image. It stands for all the blocked roads of the young generation in that society. The book was a complete failure. But in Goldzink's view, Stendhal had now found his way. He had not yet found his tone. Le Rouge et le Noir (The Red and the Black, 1830) began with a real crime. Stendhal took the main lines of his story from the case of Antoine Berthet. A law newspaper, the Gazette des Tribunaux, had reported it at the end of December 1827. Berthet was the son of a village blacksmith. He became the tutor of the children of a rich family at Brangues. He had a love affair with the mother. He was then sent to a seminary, a school for future priests. Later, Berthet fired two pistol shots at Madame Michoud, who had been his lover. He was executed by the guillotine in February 1828. Hemmings stresses that Stendhal copied only a few events from this case. Julien's character has nothing in common with Berthet's. Another model was Adrien Lafargue, a young worker from Bagnères-de-Bigorre. His murder trial fascinated Stendhal in 1829. Stendhal saw in Lafargue the same mixture as in the young Napoleon. Both were well educated, full of imagination, and very poor. Hemmings shows that Julien shares these three things. Stendhal had the idea for the novel in October 1829. He began the real work on 17 January 1830. He signed a contract with the publisher on 8 April, and he corrected the proofs in May. At first, Stendhal thought of calling the book Julien. He found the final title only in May 1830. He looked for the short quotations that open each chapter on 25 May 1830, while he was correcting the proofs. The book appeared on 13 November 1830. The publisher printed the year 1831 on the title page, as was often done at the time. On the title page, the subtitle was "Chronicle of the 19th century". At the head of the first chapter, the book was called "Chronicle of 1830". Stendhal summed up the story himself. Julien Sorel is a young peasant who has learned Latin from his priest.

Step Up is a 2006 American romantic musical teen drama movie set in Maryland. This movie is similar to "Bring It On" (which was released in 2000), except there is hip hop involved. This movie was released August 11, 2006 in the United States. The reviews were mixed to negative, though the movie had a high box office intake. The sequel, Step Up 2: The Streets, was released February 14, 2008. It stars Briana Evigan, Robert Hoffman, and Cassie and directed by Jon Chu. A second sequel called Step Up 3D was released on August 6, 2010. A third sequel called Step Up Revolution was released in 2012 and the fifth and final movie, Step Up: All In, was released in 2014.

A stencil is a blocking material used to mask a surface. In it there are holes for ink or paint to pass through. That way an image is made on the material behind the stencil. Stencils are used when many copies are needed of the same image. It is used in street art, and many public notices. Screen printing is a printing technique using a fine mesh. Ink is applied except in areas blocked by a stencil.

Stepan Andriyovych Bandera (January 1, 1909 – October 15, 1959) was a Ukrainian nationalist who co-founded the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). Bandera joined the OUN in his twenties when western Ukraine was governed by Poland, while eastern Ukraine was ruled by the Soviet Union and going through the Holodomor, a man-made famine under Joseph Stalin that killed as many as 7,000,000. The 1936 assassination of Poland's Minister of Interior caused Bandera to be sentenced to life imprisonment. He was freed by the Soviets to live in Nazi-occupied Poland after the Nazi-Soviet partition of Poland in October 1939. Factional infighting within the OUN caused the formation of the OUN-B led by him. Before the Operation Barbarossa, Bandera raised the Ukrainian Auxiliary Police for Hitler. He tried to create a Ukrainian government in Nazi-occupied Soviet Ukraine, but was deported to the Sachsenhausen concentration camp. Upon his release in September 1944, he negotiated the founding of the Ukrainian National Army (UNA) and Ukrainian National Committee (UNK) before the fall of Nazi Germany, but it had no impact on the post-war fate of the Ukrainians. Ukraine did not restore independence until 1991. Bandera and his family were resettled in Munich, West Germany. The Soviet Union asked for Bandera and several Ukrainian nationalists to be handed over under the intra-Allied cooperation wartime agreement. However, the Americans refused to hand over him. They saw him as too valuable to give up due to his knowledge of the Soviet Union useful for the Cold War. In his final years, he also visited Ukrainian exile communities in the UK, Austria, Belgium, Holland, Italy, Spain and Canada. Due to Bandera's commitment to Ukrainian liberation from Soviet imperialism, the Soviets had made several attempts on his life, which they ultimately succeeded on October 15, 1959, when Bandera died of cyanide gas poisoning on a street in Munich. During Bandera's detention in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp, the OUN-B was involved in the Volhynia massacre, killing as many as 133,000 Poles, but his role is disputed. Today, the Volhynia massacre is a controversial issue, affecting Poland–Ukraine relations and broader European politics. Both Rossolinski-Liebe and German political scientist Andreas Umland believed that Bandera was not involved in the Holocaust: Rossoliński-Liebe saw Bandera's antisemitic views as a product of his time. The view was shared by American historian Alexander John Motyl, who did not see Ukrainian nationalism as antisemitic as Nazism. Rather, the OUN-B saw the Poles and Russians as its main enemies. Bandera believed that Russian imperialism must be ended: Since Bandera's death in 1959, he has been a highly divisive figure in both Europe and America, with his legacy under intense debate, complicated by geopolitics, including the EU–Ukraine relations, Polish WWII history dispute and Ukraino–Russian war, when Putin's dictatorship keeps equating Bandera with ordinary Ukrainians to demonize Ukraine and justify the invasion. Since Ukraine restored independence in 1991, Stepan Bandera monuments have been built across western Ukraine, including the Stepan Bandera monument in Lviv. In December 2018, the Ukrainian Parliament declared January 1 as the national day of commemoration for Stepan Bandera. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine started, Stepan Bandera has reportedly been rehabilitated in Ukraine as a national hero who sacrificed for the fight against Russian imperialism, with substantial popularity among young Ukrainians. In April 2022, it is found that 74% Ukrainians had a favourable view of Stepan Bandera. On New Year's Day 2023, the Ukrainian Parliament tweeted a photo of Valeri Zaloujny, the then-Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, giving a thumbs-up to a Stepan Bandera portrait, with a caption encouraging Ukrainians to keep up the fight. Stephanie Louise Kwolek (July 31, 1923 – June 18, 2014) was an American chemist. She invented poly-paraphenylene terephthalamide—better known as Kevlar. She was born in the Pittsburgh suburb of New Kensington, Pennsylvania. Kwolek won many awards for her work in polymer chemistry. Kwolek died in Wilmington, Delaware from a short-illness, at the age 90 on June 18, 2014.

Stephanie McCrummen is an American journalist. She won a George Polk Award and Pulitzer Prize in Investigative Reporting. She graduated from University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Columbia University. She worked for The Washington Post.

Stephanie Kelton (née Bell; born October 10, 1969) is an American economist and academic. She is currently a professor at Stony Brook University and a Senior Fellow at the Schwartz Center for Economic Policy Analysis at the New School for Social Research. She was a professor at the University of Missouri–Kansas City. She also was an advisor to Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign. She is founder and editor-in-chief of the blog New Economic Perspectives.

Stephen Townley Crane (November 1, 1871 - June 5, 1900) was an American writer. He was born on November 1, 1871 in Newark, New Jersey to Jonathan Townley Crane, a clergyman, and Mary Helen Peck Crane. He attended Syracuse University in Syracuse, New York, but did not graduate. He moved to New York City in 1892 to write about the slum life of Manhattan. His major works include the novella Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893), the war novel The Red Badge of Courage (1895), and the short story "The Open Boat" (1897). After the success of Badge, his literary reputation declined. His health was poor. In May 1899, he entered a sanitarium in Badenweiler, Germany. On June 5, 1900, he died of tuberculosis. He is buried in the Evergreen Cemetery in Hillside, New Jersey.

Stephen Richards Covey (October 24, 1932 – July 16, 2012) was an American educator, author, businessman and keynote speaker. His most popular book is The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989). His other books include First Things First, Principle-Centered Leadership, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective Families, The 8th Habit and The Leader in Me: How Schools and Parents Around the World Are Inspiring Greatness, One Child At a Time. In 1996, Time magazine named him one of the 25 most influential people. At the time of his death, he was a professor at the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University. Covey was born in Salt Lake City, Utah. He was married to Sandra Covey and had nine children. He was a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In April 2012, Covey was injured in a bike accident in Provo, Utah. On July 16, 2012, he died of problems relating to the accident at a Idaho Falls, Idaho hospital. He was 79.

Stephen Anthony Smith (born October 14, 1967) is an American sports television personality, radio host and journalist. He works for ESPN. He is a commentator on ESPN's First Take. He is also an analyst for EPSN's SportsCenter. Smith was born in the Bronx, New York City. He grew up in Hollis, Queens. His parents were from Saint Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands.

Stephen William Hawking (8 January 1942 – 14 March 2018) was a British theoretical physicist and mathematician. He was born in Oxford. In 1950, he moved to St Albans, Hertfordshire. He was one of the world's leading theoretical physicists. Hawking has written many science books for people who are not scientists. Hawking was a professor of mathematics at the University of Cambridge (a position that Isaac Newton once had). He retired on 1 October 2009. Hawking had a motor neurone disease, and because of that he could not move or talk very well. The illness worsened over the years and he was almost completely paralysed. He used a wheelchair to move, and an Intel computer to talk for him. He died on 14 March 2018. Hawking went to St Albans School, a local public school in Hertfordshire. At 17, he passed an exam to study at Oxford. He studied physics and chemistry there. Because he found it really easy at the beginning, he didn't study a lot for the final exams. In October 1962 he started his graduate course at Trinity Hall. It was at this time that his illness started to show up. He had difficulties in rowing and then even simply in walking. However, he finished his PhD and wrote about black holes in his thesis. He then got a fellowship (a job as a university teacher) at Gonville and Caius College in 1965. Hawking was a cosmologist—someone who studies the structure of the universe (stars and space). He invented important theories about the Big Bang (the start of the universe), black holes and how they work. Stephen Hawking predicted that black holes eject some radiation (energy), even though they normally swallow everything. That kind of radiation is named "Hawking Radiation." Hawking also worked on the problem of quantum gravity. Quantum gravity tries to explain how gravity works with quantum mechanics (physics of tiny things.) That is a hard problem that scientists have not solved yet. Hawking also wrote popular books about science for non-scientists. His first book, A Brief History of Time, sold over ten million copies. Hawking had many other jobs as well. He was an Actor, Mathematician, etc. More info on the official site Hawking died on 14 March 2018 in Cambridge, Cambridgeshire of complications from motor neuron disease at the age of 76. His ashes are buried in Westminster Abbey in London near Charles Darwin and Isaac Newton. Singularities in Collapsing Stars and Expanding Universes, with D.W. Sciama, 1969.
