He had designed the make-up for Yoda. Freeborn was born on September 5, 1914 in Leytonstone, London, England. He was married to Kay Freeborn until her death in 2012. They had three children, all who died before him. Freeborn died on February 5, 2013 in his home in London, England from natural causes, aged 98.

Stuart Orlando Scott (July 19, 1965 – January 4, 2015) was an American sportscaster and anchor on ESPN, most notably on the network's SportsCenter. He was born in Chicago, Illinois. Scott died in Avon, Connecticut from appendix cancer aged 49.

Stuart Varney (born July 7, 1949) is a British economic journalist. Varney joined Fox News Channel in January, 2004 as a business contributor on other shows including Your World with Neil Cavuto. He joined the Fox Business Network as an anchor when the network started in October 2007. He was also a guest host and contributor for FOX News Channel's Your World with Neil Cavuto. Varney was born on July 7, 1949 in Derby, Derbyshire, England. he graduated from the London School of Economics. He started at KEMO-TV in San Francisco as a business anchor. In 1980 when CNN started, he hosted shows such as Business Day and Business Asia. On CNN’s Moneyline he co-hosted with Willow Bay from 1999 to 2001. He also worked for CNBC.

Stuart Wagstaff (13 February 1925 – 10 March 2015) was an English-born Australian entertainer. He was active in all genres of the industry including television, theatre and stage management. The Journalist (1979).... Courtney Lewers All at Sea (1977) (TV).... Mr. Arthur Pickering The Dick Emery Show in Australia (1977) TV Series.... Various Characters Is There Anybody There? (1975) (TV).... Uncredited For Pete's Sake (1974).... Man in Chandelier Store... aka July Pork Bellies Seagulls Over Sorrento (1960) (TV).... Uncredited A Night to Remember (1958).... Uncredited

Stuart Timmons (January 14, 1957 – January 28, 2017) was an American journalist, activist, and historian. He was an award-winning author specializing in LGBT history. He was the author of The Trouble With Harry Hay: Founder of the Modern Gay Movement and the co-author of Gay L.A.: A History of Sexual Outlaws, Power Politics, And Lipstick Lesbians with Lillian Faderman. In 2007, Stuart began developing walking tours of LGBTQ historic sites in Los Angeles. Timmons was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota. He studied at the University of California, Los Angeles. In 2008, he suffered a massive stroke that left him paralyzed from the waist down. Timmons died on January 28, 2017 at a hospital in Hollywood, California from cardiac arrest, at the age of 60.

Andrew Stuart McLean, OC (April 19, 1948 – February 15, 2017) was a Canadian radio broadcaster, humorist, monologist, and author. He was best known as the host of the CBC Radio program The Vinyl Cafe. He was often called as a "story-telling comic". He had written many serious stories. He was known for his voice and his ability to change his popular stories to make them different on every show. McLean was diagnosed with melanoma in November 2015. He died on February 15, 2017 from the disease in Toronto, aged 68.

Stuart Heydinger (5 May 1927 – 6 October 2019) was a British photojournalist and portrait photographer. He was chief photographer at The Observer from 1960 to 1966. Heydinger was born in Kingston upon Thames, London. Heydinger died on 6 October 2019 at the age of 92.

Stuart Allen "Stu" Roosa (August 16, 1933 – December 12, 1994), (Col., USAF), was an American aeronautical engineer, United States Air Force pilot, test pilot, and NASA astronaut. He was the Command Module Pilot for the Apollo 14 mission. He was the third mission to land astronauts (Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell) on the Moon. While Shepard and Mitchell spent two days on the lunar surface, Roosa made experiments from orbit in the Command Module Kitty Hawk. He was one of 24 men to travel to the Moon, which he orbited 34 times. Roosa died of pancreatitis in Falls Church, Virginia on December 12, 1994 at the age of 61.

John Stuart Wheeler (30 January 1935 – 23 July 2020) was a British financier and political activist. He made his fortune as the founder of the spread betting firm IG Index in 1974. He was best known for his political activism, being a major donor to the Conservative Party and treasurer of the UK Independence Party from 2011 to 2014. He was born in London. In June 2020, Wheeler announced that he had stomach cancer with only "six months to live". He died a month later on 23 July 2020 at his home in Chilham, Kent from the disease, aged 85.

Stuart Craig (14 April 1942 – 7 September 2025) was a British production designer. He designed movie sets and was known for his works with set decorator Stephenie McMillan. He was known for his works on all of the Harry Potter movies. Craig was born in Norfolk, England. Craig was nominated for eleven Academy Awards, and won three: in 1982 for Gandhi, in 1998 for Dangerous Liaisons, and in 1996 for The English Patient. Craig died from problems caused by Parkinson's disease on 7 September 2025, at the age of 83.

The Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) was a student activist movement in the United States in the 1960s (1960 to 1969). A new SDS group was also begun in 2006. SDS held its first meeting in 1960 at Ann Arbor, Michigan. They had their first convention in 1962, and criticized the political system of the United States for not bringing international peace or fixing problems in society at home. It also called for non-violent civil disobedience so that student youth could bring forth a "participatory democracy." In the school year 1962-1963, the President of SDS was Tom Hayden, who later became famous. There were nine chapters around the country with at most, about 1000 members. The national office (NO) in New York City had only a few desks, some broken chairs, a couple of filing cabinets, and a few typewriters. On October 1, 1964, the University of California, Berkeley exploded into the free speech movement. Led by a Friends of SNCC student activist named Mario Savio, more than three thousand students surrounded a police car where a student, arrested for setting up a card table against a ban by the university, was being taken away. The sit-down stopped the police car from moving for 36 hours. The demonstrations, meetings and strikes all but shut the university down. Hundreds of students were arrested. SDS leaders watched and learned from this lesson. In February 1965, US President Lyndon Johnson made the war in Vietnam much bigger by bombing North Vietnam and putting ground troops right into fighting against the Viet Cong in the South. The draft became a very real issue in the lives of students in America. Campus chapters of SDS all over the country started to lead small, local demonstrations against the war and the NO became the main group that organized the March against the war in Washington DC on April 17. The first teach-in against the war was held in the University of Michigan. Soon hundreds more, all over the country, were held. The demonstration in Washington, DC attracted about 25,000 anti-war protesters and SDS became the leading student group against the war on most U.S. campuses. The 1965 summer convention was held at Kewadin, Northern Michigan. and the National Office, moved from Manhattan to Chicago at about the same time. This brought more changes. "For the first time at an SDS meeting people smoked marijuana; Pancho Villa mustaches... blue workshirts, denim jackets, and boots were worn by both men and women. These were people generally raised outside of the East, many from the Midwest and Southwest The Winter and Spring of 1967 saw more militancy of the protests at many campuses. Harassment by the authorities was also on the rise. The hippie movement really began to take hold. The 1967 convention spoke on the draft and resisting within the Army itself, and made a call for immediate withdrawal from Vietnam. Also, a women's liberation vote was passed for the first time. That Fall saw more anti-war actions. The school year started with a large demonstration against the University of Wisconsin in Madison, Wisconsin on October 17 for letting Dow recruiters on campus. Peaceful at first, the demonstrations turned to a sit-in that was violently broken up by the Madison police and riot squad, causing many injuries and arrests. A rally and a student strike then closed the university for several days. Demonstrations against the draft led by members of the Resistance, the War Resisters League, and SDS added fuel to the fire of resistance. After regular civil rights tactics of peaceful pickets, the Oakland California Stop the Draft Week ended in mass hit and run fights with the police. The huge (100,000 people) October 21 March on the Pentagon saw hundreds arrested and hurt. Night-time raids on draft offices began to spread. In the spring of 1968, National SDS activists led an effort on the campuses called "Ten Days of Resistance" and local chapters held rallies, marches, sit-ins and teach-ins, ending in a one-day strike on April 26. About a million students stayed away from classes that day, the largest ever student strike in the history of the United States. It was mostly ignored by the New York City-based national media, which was more focused on the student shutdown of Columbia University in NYC, led by an inter-racial alliance of Columbia SDS chapter activists and Student Afro Society activists. Because of the Columbia Student Revolt, "SDS" became a household name in the United States for a few years; and membership in SDS chapters around the United States grew greatly during the 1968-69 school year. In the summer of 1969, the ninth SDS national convention was held at the Chicago Coliseum with some 2000 people attending. Many groups of the movement were there, even Communists, and set up their tables all around the edges of the hall, together with undercover spies, creating an air of excitement. Each of the delegates was given a paper saying "You don't need a Weatherman to know which way the wind blows" (a lyric from a Bob Dylan song, "Subterranean Homesick Blues"). This was written by a group who later became called the Weathermen and were involved in more violent protests. They took over by voting out another large group, the convention quickly fell apart, and so did SDS. Beginning January 2006, there is a movement to start a new SDS. A small group of old SDS members joined with a Connecticut high school student to call for a new SDS fighting for civil rights and against war. Several chapters at various colleges were later started. On Martin Luther King Day of 2006, these chapters called for the first national convention since 1969 to be held in the summer of 2006 Lately SDS has been in actions against war. The Pace University chapter of SDS protested against a speech by Bill Clinton held at the campus, causing the university to hand over two students to the United States Secret Service. When the school was going to kick these two students out of school, Pace SDS began a movement in March 2006 protesting the university's actions. On March 19 2006, SDS marched in New York City against the war in Iraq. Seventeen people were arrested at the Times Square Recruitment Center, including several SDS members. Beginning in March and continuing into April and May, SDS chapters across the country participated in the Immigrant Rights Movement. On April 29 2006 SDS was in the march for Peace, Justice and Democracy in Manhattan, NY. As of July 2006, there are 150 SDS chapters around the country and over 1000 members. The newly formed SDS held its first national convention from August 4 to August 7, 2006 at the University of Chicago.

Stuart Woods (January 9, 1938 – July 22, 2022) was an American novelist. He was known best for his first novel Chiefs and his series of novels about the Stone Barrington character. Woods died on July 22, 2022 in Washington, Connecticut at the age of 84.

Stupid was a short-lived grouping of constructivist artists, formed in Cologne in 1919. The founding members were Willy Fick, Heinrich Hoerle and his wife Angelika Hoerle (1899–1923), Anton Räderscheidt and his wife Marta Hegemann, and Franz Wilhelm Seiwert. The Stupid group aimed to address sociopolitical issues through an art of proletarian character. Seiwert and Räderscheidt were at the time active in the local Dada scene. Räderscheidt's studio was their base of operations, but by 1920 he had abandoned the constructivist style. The group exhibited together and issued a publication, "Stupid 1", before disbanding.

Sture Allén (31 December 1928 – 20 June 2022) was a Swedish linguist and professor. He worked at the University of Gothenburg. He was the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy between 1986 and 1999. He was born in Gothenburg. Allén was elected to chair 3 of the Swedish Academy in 1980. Allén was also a member of the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters. He was elected a member of the Academia Europaea in 1989. Allén died on 20 June 2022 in Gothenburg, Sweden at the age of 93.

Nicolas Antonio Sturniolo, Matthew Bernard Sturniolo, and Christopher Owen Sturniolo (born August 1, 2003) known online as the Sturniolo Triplets, are American influencers. They make videos on YouTube and are popular online. They are from Somerville, Massachusetts. In 2020, they started putting videos of themselves talking in their car online. These videos made them famous. They are also popular on TikTok, where they have more than 9 million followers. Nicolas, Matthew, and Christopher Sturniolo are triplets. They were born on August 1, 2003, in Somerville, Massachusetts. Somerville is near Boston. They were born by Caesarean section. Nick was born first, then Matt two minutes later, and Chris two minutes after Matt. Their family name, Sturniolo, comes from Italy. They have an older half-brother named Justin. Their mother, MaryLou, worked for schools in Somerville. They went to Benjamin G. Brown School for elementary school. There, they acted as Cerberus, a three-headed dog, in a play. Chris and Matt played sports like hockey and lacrosse. Their family's house burned down before their last year of high school, so they moved to an apartment. Nick is gay. He told his brothers he was gay in 2019, then told his Instagram followers in April 2020. They finished high school in 2021. The Sturniolo Triplets made their first YouTube video in October 2020. They ate food in a McDonald's parking lot, and in the video, were wearing costumes from Dollar Tree. They made videos of them talking and arguing in their car. These videos became popular. By July 2021, they had more than 25,000 subscribers. In 2022, they had over 2.5 million YouTube subscribers, over 1 million Instagram followers, and over 3.5 million TikTok followers. They also started working with WME and moved to Los Angeles. In 2023, their YouTube channel had 4 million subscribers, and their TikTok had 5 million followers. They went on a tour called the Let's Trip Tour. In March 2023, they started a podcast called Cut the Camera. By 2024, they had more than 8.8 million TikTok followers, 6.5 million YouTube subscribers, and 3 million Instagram followers. In January 2024, Nick started a lip balm brand called Space Camp Wellness. Chris has a clothing brand called Fresh Love. PinkNews said the Sturniolo Triplets are famous because of their "chaos". Boston Magazine said they were the "best YouTube power trio" of 2023. Amanda Lucidi said their "bickering" was "charming". Alyssa Giocobbe said they were "cute" and "charming". Rachel Chapman from Elite Daily said their videos feel "real". Fan videos of the triplets are also popular. They were on The Hollywood Reporters list of "most influential influencers" of 2024. Their videos were called "simple and simply hilarious". They are managed by United Talent.

Styx (formerly known as S/2012 (134340) 1 and informally as P5) is a small moon of the dwarf planet Pluto. It was discovered on June 26, 2012, using the Hubble Space Telescope. It is the fifth moon of Pluto discovered so far. The others are Charon, discovered in 1978, Nix and Hydra, which were discovered in 2005, and Kerberos, discovered in 2011. The moon was discovered using nine sets of images taken between 26 June and 9 July 2012 by Wide Field Camera 3 of the Hubble Space Telescope. NASA announced the discovery on 11 July 2012. The images were taken as part of a Hubble survey searching for potential hazards for the New Horizons mission, which went to Pluto in 2015. The discovery of the moon made scientists worried about the mission. Scientists working on New Horizons wanted it to pass just inside the orbit of Charon. However, Pluto may have had more bodies, such as dust or rings, orbiting it which cannot be found. These bodies could damage the New Horizons probe, and would mean that scientists had to change New Horizons' path so it would not be damaged. On 1 July 2015, after looking for seven weeks, scientists found there were no other bodies around Pluto, and announced that New Horizons would stay on its original path. New Horizons was not damaged, and took a picture of Styx on 13 July 2015. The moon is 10 to across. Because of its small size, it is likely to be irregular in shape. The moon is very faint, about one one-hundred-thousandth as bright as Pluto. The moon is likely to be made of water ice. Styx orbits the centre of mass of Pluto and Charon at a distance of around 46500 km. This is in between the orbits of Charon and Nix. The orbital path of the moon is very nearly circular, like the other moons of Pluto. The moon orbits in the same orbital plane as the other moons. The moon takes around 20 days to orbit Pluto. The moon system around Pluto may exist because of a collision of Pluto with a large Kuiper belt body a very long time ago. Pluto’s moons may have formed from the scattered pieces of rock left behind after the collision.

Stylianos Harkianakis (; 29 December 1935 – 25 March 2019) was an Australian Greek Orthodox priest. He served as the Archbishop of Australia at the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia. He moved to Australia in 1975. He taught spirituality at the University of Sydney. He was a theologian that focused on ecclesiology. He was also an award-winning poet. Harkianakis was born in Rethymno, on the island of Crete. Harkianakis died after a long illness in Sydney, New South Wales on 25 March 2019. He was 83.

Stéphane Richard (born 24 August 1961) is the former chairman and CEO of Orange S.A.. He graduated from HEC Paris and the École nationale d'administration. He studied at HEC Paris and École nationale d'administration in Strasbourg. He has also worked in politics with Christine Lagarde.

Stéphane Mallarmé (18 March 1842 – 9 September 1898) was a French poet, teacher, translator, and critic. His birth name was Étienne Mallarmé, but he used the name Stéphane for his writing. He became one of the main poets of Symbolism. Symbolism was an art movement that used images, sounds, and signs to suggest ideas and feelings. It did not try to describe the visible world in a plain and direct way. Mallarmé wrote only a small number of poems, but his work changed the history of poetry. He wanted every word to do several things at the same time. A word could name an object, but it could also bring other words, sounds, memories, and ideas into the reader's mind. For this reason, his poems often have more than one possible meaning. Their grammar can also be difficult to follow. Mallarmé believed that a poem should not explain an object directly. Instead, it should slowly make the idea of the object appear in the reader's mind. His best-known works include the unfinished dramatic poem Hérodiade, the monologue L'Après-midi d'un faune (The Afternoon of a Faun), the prose work Igitur, and the page poem Un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard (A Throw of the Dice Will Never Do Away with Chance). In this last work, Mallarmé used letters of different sizes and large areas of empty paper. The reader must look at the whole pair of pages as well as read the words. The poem became an important early example of visual poetry. Mallarmé also had a strong influence on music, painting, theatre, and dance. Édouard Manet was his friend and made pictures for two of his books. Claude Debussy used The Afternoon of a Faun as the starting point for a famous work for orchestra. Vaslav Nijinsky later created a ballet from the poem and Debussy's music. Mallarmé also wrote about Richard Wagner, modern theatre, ballet, and the new painting of his time. He did not believe that poetry should simply copy music. He wanted poetry to use the full power of language. This included meaning, sound, rhythm, silence, and the shape of the words on the printed page. For much of his life, Mallarmé worked as an English teacher. His public life seemed quiet, but his inner life and his writing were not quiet. He spent many years working on texts that he never finished. He also planned a great work called Le Livre (The Book). It would have brought together poetry, reading, theatre, and a public ceremony. Only plans and notes for this work remain. Mallarmé held meetings at his home on Tuesday evenings. These meetings were known as the Mardis. They made him an important figure in the artistic life of Paris at the end of the nineteenth century. Younger writers such as Paul Valéry, André Gide, and Paul Claudel came to listen to him there. Mallarmé was born in Paris on 18 March 1842. His father, Numa-Florent-Joseph Mallarmé, worked in the French government office that kept records of land and property. His mother was Élisabeth-Félicie Desmolins. People on both sides of the family had worked for the government for many years. The family expected the boy to enter the same kind of career. His mother died in 1847, when he was five years old. His father married Anne-Hubertine Mathieu the next year. Mallarmé spent much of his childhood with relatives or in boarding schools. He was very close to his younger sister, Maria. She died in 1857 at the age of thirteen. These early deaths do not explain all of Mallarmé's poetry in a simple way. However, the lost mother, the dead sister, the lonely child, and the empty family home appear again in some of his early poems and prose poems. He first studied near Paris and later at the school in Sens. He was not an excellent pupil in most subjects. He did well in English, French writing, and some classical subjects. He also began to write poetry. His early poems followed writers such as Alphonse de Lamartine, Victor Hugo, Théophile Gautier, and Charles Baudelaire. These first poems show a young writer copying poets whom he admired. They do not show that he already had a complete theory of poetry. Mallarmé found his own style slowly. The death of his sister had an important place in his first poems. Another young friend, Harriet Smyth, died in 1859. Mallarmé wrote poems about graves, angels, memory, and the hope of life after death. At this time, he still used the language of Christianity. Later, his religious belief became less certain. However, religious forms remained important in his thought. He continued to think about ceremony, sacrifice, death, rebirth, and a group of people joined together by a shared act. Mallarmé failed his first school-leaving examination in August 1860. He passed it in November. He then worked for a short time in a government office. He disliked the future that his family had planned for him. Poetry had already become the centre of his life. Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal gave the young Mallarmé a new model. Baudelaire showed that modern poetry could bring together beauty, illness, boredom, desire, city life, and death. At first, Mallarmé borrowed many of Baudelaire's images and tones. He later moved away from direct copying, but Baudelaire remained one of the poets whom he respected most. Edgar Allan Poe became another major influence. Mallarmé knew Poe through Baudelaire's French translations. Poe's essays described a poem as the result of careful work, not only of sudden inspiration. This idea helped Mallarmé bring together poetic feeling and careful method, choice, correction, and planning. He came to believe that a poet must work as both a dreamer and a maker. In 1862, Mallarmé met Maria Christina Gerhard, a young German woman who worked as a companion. She was older than he was. They travelled to London so that Mallarmé could improve his English and gain a teaching qualification. Their first stay was difficult, and Maria returned to France for a time. Mallarmé returned to France in 1863 and later went back to England with Maria. They married on 10 August 1863. During his studies in England, he began translating Poe. He later translated many of Poe's poems into French, including The Raven. Mallarmé's translations were important for his own poetry. English word order and Poe's patterns of sound made him think about what the French language could do. Translation also showed him that a word in one language does not always have one complete and exact partner in another language. A translator must choose between several possible meanings and effects. Mallarmé later placed the same kind of pressure on the words in his own poems. Late in 1863, Mallarmé became an assistant English teacher at the school in Tournon-sur-Rhône. He and Maria lived there with little money. Their daughter, Geneviève, was born on 19 November 1864. Mallarmé found classroom work tiring and often painful. He had a quiet voice and found it difficult to control noisy groups of boys. School reports often judged him to be a weak teacher. He also had to prepare lessons and correct work after the school day. This left him little time for poetry. Even so, the years at Tournon were very important for his writing. He wrote at night and developed a slow method of correcting and changing his work. He began Hérodiade in 1864. In 1865, he began the work that later became L'Après-midi d'un faune. He also wrote prose poems such as Le Démon de l'analogie (The Demon of Analogy). In a letter from this period, Mallarmé said that he wanted to show not the thing itself, but the effect that it produces. This became one of the clearest statements of his early poetic method. In 1866, eleven of his poems appeared in the first volume of Le Parnasse contemporain. This book brought together poets connected with Parnassianism. The Parnassian poets valued careful form, distance from private feeling, and exact artistic work. Mallarmé shared these aims, but he soon moved beyond them. He wanted a poem to create an unseen order through the relations between its words. Mallarmé's crisis began while he was still teaching at Tournon in the spring of 1866. Letters from this time describe illness, lack of sleep, fear that he could no longer write, the loss of religious faith, and an encounter with what he called le Néant, or Nothingness. Later in 1866, he moved to Besançon, and in 1867 to Avignon. The word Néant does not mean only empty despair. It can also mean the removal of easy beliefs and meanings that are already prepared. Poetry would have to begin again after this loss. Critics have explained this crisis in different ways. Guy Michaud gives it an important place in Mallarmé's search for a new kind of poetry. Charles Chadwick studies the movement of thought inside the poems and letters. The evidence also shows that Mallarmé suffered a personal and artistic breakdown. Mallarmé did not stop writing after the crisis. Instead, he changed his idea of the poet. The poet was no longer only a person who expressed private feelings. The poet became a worker who allowed language to create relations that were larger than one human life. During the same period, Mallarmé wrote parts of Igitur. Its young hero enters a dark family house at midnight. He tries to complete an act that will defeat chance, but the work remains unfinished. The text is at the same time a family story, a test of ideas, an action for the stage, and a study of writing. Its unfinished form is part of its importance in literary history. Mallarmé's son Anatole was born on 16 July 1871. In the same year, the family moved to Paris. Mallarmé taught at the Lycée Fontanes, now called the Lycée Condorcet. He later taught at the Lycée Janson-de-Sailly and the Collège Rollin. In all, he worked as a teacher for about thirty years. Paris gave him a larger circle of writers and artists. He became a close friend of Manet. He also knew Berthe Morisot, James McNeill Whistler, Odilon Redon, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and other artists. These friendships were not only social. Mallarmé thought deeply about painting, books, pictures in books, and the place of art in modern life. In 1874, Mallarmé wrote and edited a fashion magazine called La Dernière Mode (The Latest Fashion). Only eight issues were published. He wrote most of the magazine himself, using several different names, including names that appeared to belong to women. He wrote about clothes, theatre, food, travel, the design of homes, and social behaviour. The magazine shows a playful side of Mallarmé. It also shows his interest in surfaces, objects, style, and the modern press. He could write clear and practical prose when the subject required it. In 1874, the family began spending holidays at Valvins, near the Forest of Fontainebleau. The small house beside the Seine became one of the most important places in Mallarmé's life. He sailed, worked in the garden, received friends, and wrote there. The quiet river landscape entered his prose and letters. Valvins was not a complete escape from society. It was a place where private work and friendly meetings could exist together. In 1875, the family moved to 87 rue de Rome in Paris. This apartment later became famous because of the Tuesday meetings held there. In 1875, Mallarmé also published his translation of Poe's The Raven, with pictures by Manet. In 1876, he published L'Après-midi d'un faune in a small and costly edition, again with pictures by Manet. Manet painted Mallarmé's portrait in the same year. Mallarmé did not become rich from these books. Many editions were small and expensive. They reached artists and collectors more easily than ordinary readers. However, they helped to create a new kind of book in which the paper, printed letters, pictures, and poem formed one complete work of art. Anatole became ill and died in 1879, at the age of eight. Mallarmé began writing notes for a work about his son. These notes are known as Pour un tombeau d'Anatole (For Anatole's Tomb). He never turned them into a finished book. The notes are broken, painful, and often very direct. They show a father trying to think about death without changing his grief into an easy religious answer. Around 1880, the Tuesday evening meetings at the apartment in rue de Rome became regular. They were called the Mardis, from the French word for Tuesday. Visitors came without much formal planning. Mallarmé often stood near the fireplace, smoked, and spoke in a quiet voice. His writing could be difficult, but people often found his speech clear, graceful, and amusing. His movements and tone of voice helped listeners understand ideas that seemed more difficult on the printed page. The group changed over time. It included older friends such as Paul Verlaine, Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, and Joris-Karl Huysmans. Younger visitors included Gide, Valéry, Claudel, Henri de Régnier, and Pierre Louÿs. Writers and artists from other countries also came. The meetings brought together several generations and several kinds of art. Mallarmé became known as le Maître, or the Master. However, he did not lead a school with fixed rules. He encouraged different writers to find their own style and form. In 1883, the magazine Lutèce began publishing Verlaine's studies of the writers whom he called Les Poètes maudits (The Accursed Poets). His study of Mallarmé was part of this series. Verlaine collected the first studies in a book in 1884. This helped to make Mallarmé better known. Manet died in 1883, and his death affected Mallarmé deeply. During the 1880s, younger Symbolist writers increasingly saw Mallarmé as a leading poet. His reputation grew even though much of his work remained unpublished, unfinished, or available only in rare editions. Mallarmé stopped teaching at the end of 1893, after about thirty years of work. In 1894, he gave the lecture La Musique et les Lettres (Music and Letters) in England. He spoke at Oxford and Cambridge. The text was published in 1895. The lecture brought together many of his later ideas about poetry, music, nature, society, and books. Debussy's Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune was first performed in 1894. At first, Mallarmé was uncertain about a musical work based on his poem. He later accepted it warmly. Debussy did not simply retell the poem's story. He created a new musical movement from its mood, pauses, desire, and uncertain dream. After Verlaine died in 1896, a vote among writers named Mallarmé the new Prince of Poets. The title was not official, but it showed his high position in French literary life. In 1897, Mallarmé published Divagations, a carefully ordered book of prose. In the same year, the magazine Cosmopolis published Un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard. The magazine could not follow all of Mallarmé's plans for the size of the letters and the design of the pages, but the main visual idea was already clear. Mallarmé continued to work on Hérodiade, The Book, and other plans. On 8 September 1898, he suffered a serious attack in his throat at Valvins. In a final note to his wife Maria and his daughter Geneviève, he clearly asked them to burn the large number of unfinished notes that he was leaving behind. He wrote that only he could have used them and that they were not a literary inheritance. He died the next day, on 9 September, and was buried at Samoreau, near Valvins. His family did not destroy all his papers. Important notes survived, although no complete version of The Book has ever been found. Mallarmé did not accept the simple idea that a poet only waits for inspiration. Feelings were important to him, but they were only the beginning. A poem needed long and careful work. He often changed the same poem over many years. He changed single words, punctuation, the order of lines, and even the place of a poem inside a book. Several of his main works exist in both early and later forms. This method came partly from Poe. Poe had described the writing of a poem as a planned process. Mallarmé did not copy Poe's method in a mechanical way. He joined careful planning with uncertainty. The poet can choose words and forms, but the work may also create relations that the poet did not fully plan. Writing therefore takes place between control and chance. Claude Abastado describes this double movement as an important part of Mallarmé's theory of creation. The poet is both a careful worker and a performer on a stage. He knows that art uses methods, masks, and effects. At the same time, he wants the finished work to seem free from the hard work that created it. Images of the actor, clown, and juggler appear many times in Mallarmé's writing. Mallarmé worked slowly, but this was not only because he was afraid of failure. He believed that every new work should test a new part of language. He did not want to repeat an easy success. This helps to explain why he wrote only a small number of poems, although they are very different from one another. His works include traditional sonnets, dramatic speeches, prose poems, short poems written in memory of the dead, critical prose, and a large visual poem. In ordinary speech, a person usually names something in order to give information. Mallarmé described much ordinary writing as a kind of universal reporting. A newspaper report, a school lesson, and a practical message may all use words as clear signs. Poetry has a different purpose. It does not only carry a fact from one person to another. Mallarmé often said that poetry should suggest. To suggest means to lead the mind towards something without giving it completely and at once. A poem may begin with a flower, a fan, a window, a swan, or a star. The object does not remain only a simple object. Its links with other words slowly create a larger idea. The reader takes part in creating this idea. This does not mean that Mallarmé wanted writing to be unclear without purpose. His best poems are very exact in their sound and structure. They are difficult because they hold many relations together. A direct statement closes many possible paths. Suggestion keeps several paths open. The flower is a useful example. A real flower has a colour, a smell, and a place. The word flower has no petals. However, it can bring many flowers into the mind, including flowers that are not present. Mallarmé valued this power of absence. A poem can make an ideal flower appear through language without copying one particular plant in a garden. For Mallarmé, a word is a meeting place. Its dictionary meaning is only one part of it. The poet also uses its sound, its older meanings, its place in a sentence, its links with nearby words, and its visual form on the page. One word may bring several images into the mind at the same time. French words often have several possible sounds and meanings. Mallarmé used these differences with great care. He liked sounds that almost repeat one another, hidden likenesses, and words that seem to answer each other. He also used rhyme as a way of thinking. Two rhyming words do not only sound alike. Their similar sound may make the reader compare their meanings. Jean Royère defended this kind of writing against people who said that it was only dark or secret. For Royère, Mallarmé made poetry think through rhythm, images, and relations between words rather than through the clear steps of an argument. A poem is not a damaged form of normal prose. It is a different use of language. Mallarmé sometimes chose a rare word because it brought several meanings together. At other times, he placed ordinary words in an unusual order. When reading his poems, a difficult word should not always be replaced by an easier one. Its exact strangeness may be part of the poem. In an article about Mallarmé, however, rare words should be clearly explained. Syntax is the order in which words form a sentence. Mallarmé often changes normal French syntax. He may place an important verb near the end of a sentence. He may separate a noun from the words that describe it. He may also leave out a word that the reader must add in the mind. This leaving out is called ellipsis. These methods make the reader move more slowly. They also change the order in which an idea appears. A normal sentence may first say who acts, then what the person does, and finally what the action affects. A sentence by Mallarmé may first present a light, a sound, or a movement. The person or object may appear only later. The reader first receives an effect and then has to search for its cause. His punctuation is also active. A dash may open another possible meaning. Brackets may place one thought inside another. A colon may turn an image into an explanation or turn an explanation into another image. In Un coup de dés, the empty paper can do the work that punctuation normally does in a paragraph. This kind of syntax is one reason why Mallarmé is difficult to translate. An English translation can make the grammar clear, but it may then remove the uncertainty found in the French. A translation that follows the French word order may keep more of the poem's movement, but it may sound strange in English. The translators of Guy Michaud's study chose to keep many of these planned uncertainties instead of turning the poems into simple explanations. Romantic poetry often presents a strong personal speaker. Mallarmé used personal feelings, but he wanted the writer's ordinary self to move away from the centre of the poem. He spoke about the poet disappearing as a person from the work. This idea is often called poetic impersonality. Impersonality does not mean that the poems have no emotion. For Anatole's Tomb came from a private loss. Brise marine came from a wish to escape a dull life. The swan sonnet gives a powerful image of failure. However, the poems turn these private feelings into forms that are not limited to one person's life. The speaking voice may be a faun, a princess, a dead poet, a clown, a swan, a priest, or an unnamed watcher. These figures work like masks. A mask hides one face, but it also makes another form visible. Wallace Fowlie therefore studies Mallarmé through several poetic masks, including the clown, the swan, and the hero. The poem itself may also seem to speak. Words answer other words through sound and form. In this sense, the poet does not disappear completely. He gives up direct control so that a larger order of words can appear. Mallarmé often used the word Ideal. In his writing, it does not simply mean a perfect thing that a person would like to have. It may mean an unseen form or relation that art makes present. A group of real flowers dies. The poetic idea of the flower is not one physical plant. It is created through all the relations that the poem gives to the word. The Ideal has a difficult relation with the real world. The poet may desire pure beauty and reject daily life. This desire may become a trap. In L'Azur, the blue sky first appears as a sign of the Ideal. Later, it becomes an unbearable force that follows the poet. In the swan sonnet, the bird remembers a flight that it cannot make. Its pure white body is trapped in frozen water. Nothingness is the other side of the Ideal. If a poem removes the solid object, what remains? Mallarmé sometimes answers that an idea, a relation, a sound, or a blank remains. At other times, Nothingness is frightening. It may mean the loss of God, the fear that language has no final support, or the possibility that the work will never be finished. Guy Michaud presents Mallarmé's world as a web. Every part receives meaning through its links with the other parts. The web has no single solid centre. This model helps to explain why the Ideal and Nothingness are not simple opposites. Removing a fixed object may open a new field of relations. Mallarmé did not believe that art gives scientific facts. Art creates a fiction. A fiction is not only a lie. It is a created form through which people can see relations that ordinary life hides. His later works often use an as if movement. A poem may present a shipwreck as if it had happened, a constellation as if it were forming, or a public ceremony as if it could join a crowd together. The reader knows that the scene is made from words. Even so, the reader enters it for a time. This double knowledge is central to Mallarmé's art. Art needs belief, but not blind belief. A theatre audience knows that the stage is not ordinary life. However, the shared act may still change the way the audience sees life. Paula Gilbert Lewis argues that Mallarmé's art depends on this free participation by the public. The work cannot force belief. Its power begins when readers or viewers agree to enter the fiction. Chance is one of Mallarmé's main subjects. A word enters a language through history. A life begins in one family rather than another. A throw of dice produces one number from many possible numbers. The poet wants to create a necessary form from material that includes chance. Igitur presents a young man who tries to end the power of chance through one final act. The act does not bring a simple victory. Many years later, Un coup de dés returns to the same problem. Its title says that one throw of dice will never abolish chance. However, the throw still matters. It makes one form appear for a moment, even though it cannot remove all the other possibilities. This is also an image of the poem. The writer chooses one word, one line, and one form for the page. Other choices remain possible. The finished poem is therefore both necessary and fragile. It is a real act inside a world of chance. Mary Lewis Shaw understands this relation as a performance. The act has meaning because it happens, fails, and leaves a sign. The printed work records a movement, but it also asks the reader to perform the poem again with the eyes and the voice. For about thirty years, Mallarmé spoke and wrote about a great work called Le Livre, or The Book. He did not mean an ordinary single volume. The project changed over time. It was to bring together poetry, numbers, the order of pages, spoken reading, movement, and a public ceremony. The notes for The Book include plans for numbers of pages, groups of readers, changes of place, and repeated performances. Some notes imagine a person who reads and arranges the work before a small public. The order of the pages could change. One reading would be only one part of a larger group of possible readings. The project has often been called impossible. Mallarmé never completed it. It should not be understood as a lost perfect book that once existed fully in his mind. The surviving notes are experiments. They show him testing how a book could become an event. Mary Lewis Shaw sees in these plans a movement from art towards ritual. Reading would no longer remain a private act performed by one person. It would become a shared performance. The poet would act less like a famous writer and more like a person leading a ceremony. The Book also answers Mallarmé's concern with society. Modern life separates people into workers, buyers, readers, and watchers. A true poetic ceremony might allow a group to see itself as a whole. This hope exists beside another fact: Mallarmé's real books often reached only a small and educated public. The tension between the small group and a public open to everyone never fully disappears. Jean-Pierre Richard studied Mallarmé's poetry as an imagined world made from images, movements, materials, and shapes that return again and again. The same images appear in different works, but their meanings change each time. Sky, glass, water, ice, hair, jewels, flowers, fans, wings, paper, and stars form a connected network. The reader should not give each image one fixed meaning. Its meaning comes from its place in the whole poem. The blue sky often represents height, purity, and a world beyond ordinary life. It can draw the poet upwards. However, it can also become cruel. In L'Azur, the speaker tries to escape from the blue sky by hiding in work, smoke, and ordinary things. The sky returns as a repeated cry. The Ideal has become a power that judges the poet. Height does not therefore always mean freedom. A high window may open towards another life, but it may also separate a sick person from the world. A tower may give a wide view, but it may also leave the writer alone. Mallarmé's poetry often places desire between a clear space above and a heavy room below. A window forms a border. A person can look through it without passing through it. In Les Fenêtres, a sick man turns away from the hospital room and looks towards the light outside. The glass promises escape, but it also keeps him inside. Ships and the sea give this desire a more active form. Brise marine begins with the feeling that the body and books have become tiring. The speaker dreams of leaving. The sea is open, dangerous, and free. However, the poem itself remains on the page. The journey takes place through language. A ship may later become an image of failure. In Un coup de dés, a shipwreck spreads across a great sea. The master may hold dice in his hand, but the storm and chance surround him. Escape, danger, and the act of writing come together. Flowers have a long history in lyric poetry. Mallarmé uses them as natural objects, gifts, signs of women, and images of poetic language. A flower can be cut from its root and placed in a bouquet. In the same way, the poet takes words from ordinary speech and places them in a new order. The bouquet brings both loss and gain. The real plant is no longer present. In its place, the poem gives a group of relations. Mallarmé's famous idea of a flower that is absent from every real bouquet expresses this movement. Poetry does not destroy the world. It changes the way the world becomes present. Hair in Mallarmé's poetry can form a rich inner space. It moves like water, smoke, cloth, or music. It may hide a face or lead towards a secret centre. Richard reads hair, woods, grass, and other thick natural forms as spaces that both stop and invite movement. Cloth appears as flags, curtains, dresses, and sails. It can cover a body, catch the air, or show a public sign. The fan is a small but important object. It opens and closes. It moves the air. Its folds are like the folds of a book. Mallarmé wrote short poems on real fans for women whom he knew. The fan became at the same time a gift, a page, a wing, and an image of desire. The swan is one of Mallarmé's best-known images. In the sonnet usually called Le Cygne, a swan is trapped in ice. It remembers that it should have flown away before winter. Its white body almost becomes part of the white frozen world. The swan may represent the poet who desires a pure song but cannot complete it. It may also represent the poem itself: beautiful, silent, fixed, and trapped in its own purity. The image is powerful because it does not lead to only one lesson. In other poems, wings suggest flight, angels, birds, fans, and pages. They promise freedom. However, they may also be folded, broken, or only imagined. Mallarmé keeps the movement between rising and falling active. Mallarmé wrote much of his poetry late at night after his teaching work. The lamp was therefore a real object in his daily life. It also creates a small circle of light inside the darkness. The page appears under this light. Night may represent fear, death, or silence. It may also be a space where a new form becomes visible. Igitur takes place at midnight. Its candles, clock, old room, and family shadows turn thought into an action on a stage. Fowlie calls this part of Mallarmé's work a metaphysics of night. Night becomes a way to think about existence, absence, and the poet's act. Stars are points of light separated by darkness. The mind joins them together into a constellation. This is close to Mallarmé's idea of reading. Words are separate marks, and the reader creates relations between them across the white space. At the end of Un coup de dés, the possible constellation does not remove chance. It gives chance a temporary form. Paper is not only an empty support in Mallarmé's work. Its whiteness is active. A printed word cuts into it. An empty space may separate, delay, or connect groups of words. A folded sheet forms pages, but it also hides part of the text until the reader turns it. Mallarmé thought carefully about the physical form of a book. He cared about margins, printed letters, the quality of the paper, and the order of the pages. A closed book keeps a possible world hidden. An open book reveals that world little by little. The fold makes reading an action that takes place through time. In Un coup de dés, white space becomes part of the poem's rhythm. It may suggest silence, sea, sky, distance, or the space between thoughts. It does not have one fixed meaning. It gives the words room to form groups and movements. Mallarmé published much less than many other major poets. He revised his work slowly, left several large projects unfinished, and often published in small magazines or rare books. However, the small amount of published work can give a false idea of its importance. The same poem may exist in several versions, and a short text may contain ideas developed over many years. His letters, essays, translations, fashion writing, and notes are also important parts of his work. One useful way to study his works is to follow their dates and their different forms. His early lyric poems begin with models from Romantic and Parnassian poetry. His dramatic poems test different voices and forms of theatre. His prose poems bring the poet into the modern street, fair, concert hall, and newspaper world. His later sonnets make language very dense. Finally, Un coup de dés changes the form of the printed page itself. Mallarmé's early poems include Le Guignon (Bad Luck), Apparition, Les Fenêtres, L'Azur, Brise marine, and Les Fleurs. Most of them were written during the 1860s. They use regular metre, rhyme, and the rich images of French lyric poetry. They also introduce the main conflicts that remained in Mallarmé's work: the wish to escape ordinary life, the fear of failing as an artist, the attraction of beauty, and the knowledge that beauty can be cold or impossible to reach. Le Guignon presents poets as unlucky travellers. Some fail before they reach their goal. Others become public entertainers or failed figures. The poem uses the old idea of the rejected poet, but it does not present failure as simply noble. Failure can also be comic, ugly, and physical. Apparition is more gentle and graceful. A memory of a young woman becomes a scene filled with moonlight, flowers, and a fairy-like figure. The poem still uses a clear personal voice. However, the woman is already less important than the changing world of light, smell, colour, and memory around her. Les Fenêtres presents a sick man in a hospital. He turns away from the room and looks at the sky through a window. At first, the poem seems to place the spirit against the body. Its ending is less clear. The speaker dreams of breaking the glass and flying away, but he also fears falling back into ordinary life. The window gives him a view of freedom, but not a real way out. L'Azur turns the blue sky into an enemy. The poet tries to hide from it beneath smoke, heavy curtains, and daily work. However, the blue sky returns in his mind and in the poem's final repeated cry. The poem is important because the Ideal is not shown as a peaceful heaven. It becomes a demand that the poet cannot satisfy. Brise marine begins with one of Mallarmé's clearest statements: the body is sad, and the speaker has read all the books. He dreams of leaving by ship. The sea wind is both real and literary. It promises another place, but the poem never says that the journey truly begins. The act of leaving takes place through verse. In these poems, Mallarmé still uses many subjects also found in Baudelaire and the Parnassian poets. His own method appears in the importance given to every image. Sky, window, book, sail, flower, and wing are not only decorations. Each image takes part in a group of opposite movements: rising and falling, opening and closing, purity and the failure to create, freedom and being held back. Mallarmé worked on Hérodiade during most of his adult life. He began it in 1864 and was still changing it shortly before his death. The work takes its name from Herodias, but Mallarmé changed the old story. His Hérodiade is a young princess who refuses ordinary love and protects a cold beauty that needs nothing outside itself. The finished and unfinished parts include an opening scene, a long conversation between Hérodiade and her nurse, a song by John the Baptist, and later plans for a larger mystery play. The best-known part is the Scène, the conversation between Hérodiade and the nurse. The nurse wants to touch or care for the young woman. Hérodiade refuses. She wants to remain complete in herself. Mirrors, jewels, metal, hair, perfume, cold, and dawn create a closed world around her. Several critics have understood Hérodiade as a figure for pure poetry. Fowlie and Block also explain why this idea is not simple. Hérodiade represents both the beauty and the danger of artistic separation. She protects herself from time, touch, birth, and change. However, this protection can become a form of death. Her purity gives her power, but it prevents her from forming a relation with another person. The dramatic form is important. Hérodiade does not explain her ideas in an essay. Her thoughts appear through her voice, movements, surroundings, and conflict with the nurse. Haskell M. Block argues that Mallarmé's dramatic writing helped later Symbolist theatre move away from ordinary action and towards inner states, repeated images, and speech that sounds like a ceremony. The work also changed as Mallarmé himself changed. The early parts belong to his crisis of the 1860s. The later plans give a larger place to John the Baptist, death, sacrifice, and possible rebirth. Because Mallarmé never completed the work, readers should not force all its parts into one final system. Its long history shows several stages in the development of his art. L'Après-midi d'un faune is a dramatic monologue. Its speaker is a faun, a creature from ancient myth that is half human and half goat. He wakes at noon and tries to remember whether he met two nymphs or only dreamed about them. He plays a flute, tells parts of the event again, changes his story, imagines new scenes, and finally returns to sleep. The poem began in 1865 as a work for the theatre. Mallarmé first called it Le Faune, interlude héroïque, and later Monologue d'un faune. Theatre managers refused its early forms. Mallarmé continued revising the poem and published its best-known version in 1876. The action is uncertain from the first line. The faun says that he wants to keep the nymphs alive. It is not clear whether he means alive in memory, in song, or in desire. His senses give him signs, but these signs do not prove that the event happened. A white shape may be a woman's body, light on plants, or foam. A sound may be a cry, a bird, or music. The poem does not ask the reader to discover one correct version of the event. Its subject is the creation of an imagined event from incomplete signs. The faun is both a lover and an artist. His flute changes breath into music. His speech changes desire into poetry. He often changes failure into a new performance. When he cannot hold the nymphs, he holds their possible image. When his memory grows weak, language begins again. The poem also tests the classical French alexandrine. Its lines keep the traditional twelve syllables, but they use pauses, questions, broken phrases, and changes of voice. The result is both formal and free. Wallace Fowlie describes the poem as one of Mallarmé's richest studies of the relation between sexual desire, dreams, and poetic creation. Debussy's orchestral Prélude helped to make the poem known outside France. Nijinsky's ballet of 1912 gave the faun a new physical form.

Su Bai (; 3 August 1922 – 1 February 2018) was a Chinese archaeologist. He was born in Shenyang, Liaoning Province. He served as the first head of the Department of Archaeology of Peking University from 1983 to 1988. He was known for his pioneering research in the archaeology of Buddhism. He won the Lifetime Achievement Award from the Chinese Archaeology Society in 2016. On 1 February 2018, Su Bai died in Beijing, at the age of 95.

Su Yu-chang (; 24 June 1940 – 29 April 2019) was a Chinese martial artist, scholar and physician. He spent his life teaching Kung Fu, traditional Chinese philosophy and medicine all over the world. He was born in Dongshan, Taiwan. Su died at a hospital in La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain on 29 April 2019, aged 78.

Su Beng (9 November 1918 – 20 September 2019), whose given name was Shih Chao-hui, was a Taiwanese dissident and political activist. He was born in Shirin Town, Taihoku Chō, Japanese Taiwan (modern-day Shilin District of Taipei, Taiwan). He was known as the “Che Guevara of Taiwan". In April 1994, he began the Taiwan Independence Action motorcade, which he conceived as a way to raise the Taiwanese people’s political awareness. He fought for Taiwanese independence. Su died in Taipei on 20 September 2019 of pneumonia at the age of 100.

Submitters are followers of the Egyptian-American biochemist Rashad Khalifa (d. 1990) who established United Submitters International (USI) in Tucson, Arizona. The Submitters reject hadith and believe in the "Qur'an alone" plus the specific mathematical code (19), which Khalifa popularised, whom they consider a "Messenger of the Covenant". Though similar to Qur'anists, the Submitters do not consider themselves to be Qur'anists, as the two are fundamentally different in their core beliefs, specifically regarding the status of Khalifa and the understanding of certain practices. Qur'anists have accused Khalifa of "extremism in lying and extremism in disbelief". Masjid Tucson was a private house at Tucson, Arizona, which Khalifa rented out from a private owner to enable the Friday gatherings of Submitters back in the 1980s. People would gather there every Friday to listen to Khalifa's sermons in the 1980s. After Khalifa, it was abandoned, and now is simply a private home and the Submitters do not gather to pray there anymore. Today, the Submitters are thinly spread throughout the world and gather mainly online. The USI founded by Khalifa has published a monthly newsletter with the title "Submitter's Perspective" since 1985. Among those influenced by Khalifa's ideas include Edip Yüksel, Ahmad Rashad, and Nigerian High Court Judge, Isa Othman.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (19 October 1910 – 21 August 1995) was an Indian Physicist. He received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside William Alfred Fowler "for his theoretical studies of the physical processes of importance to the structure and evolution of the stars". He was born in Lahore now Pakistan until 1916, his family came and settled in Allahabad then in 1918, moved to Madras. He died in Chicago.

the Subsistence Principle is one of the Three Principles of the People (Nationalism, Democracy and Subsistence) created by Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925). The objective of the Subsistence is end the class struggle without deaths, promote a mixed socialist economy and reach the "social and economic justice" (Equality in the economic and the society). The Subsistence do not support the communism and the marxism. For Sun, the mixed economy is fundamental in for the socioeconomic justice. The tridemist state, need to balance between the planned economy and the market economy. Sun considered that in this way, because with the people's party in government, social classes could be easily regulated with the land redistribution, to control over the monopoly of private properties and the means of production without apply a communist state or killing peoples. Currently, Taiwan and Singapore, nations under a tridemist government, have regulations on land and property, usually breaking up or limiting large monopolies. In China, the Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, formulated by Deng Xiaoping, comes very close to Sun's original idea of building a balanced economy.

Suchitra Bhattacharya (10 January 1950 – 12 May 2015) was an Indian novelist. Over the past two decades, Suchitra had written about 24 novels and a large number of short stories in different leading Bengali literary magazines. Bhattacharya died on 12 May 2015 from cardiac arrest at her home in Dhakuria, Kolkata, aged 65.

Subzero (nickname: Subbie) (foaled 26 September 1988 in Australia 29 August 2020) was a Thoroughbred racehorse. Subzero won the 1992 Melbourne Cup. Trained by Lee Freedman and ridden by veteran jockey Greg Hall, the four-year-old revelled in the rain-affected going to defeat the favourite Veandercross and the two-miler Castletown. The win was to be Subzero's last, but, as one of the few grey winners of the race in the post-War era, his fame was assured. Upon retirement from racing, the big, near-white gelding with a lovely temperament was employed as the clerk of the course's horse by Racing Victoria's long-time Clerk, Graham Salisbury, and has made numerous appearances on television, at charity functions, and at schools. In July 2008, he was fully retired as he had developed arthritis. In October 2009, it was reported that Subzero might need to be put down as the medication he needed for his arthritis became unavailable in Australia. However the medication was subsequently sourced from the United States, and Subzero continued to appear in public. In his retirement he was gentle natured, very patient with children and remained with Graham Salisbury until Salisbury's death in June 2020. On 29 August 2020, he was humanely put down due to a heart condition. He was 31.

Suchir Balaji (November 21, 1998 – November 26, 2024) was an American artificial intelligence researcher. He died several weeks after accusing his former employer, OpenAI, of breaking United States copyright law. Balaji's death received wide attention because his parents and others said there might have been foul play, and because he was seen as a whistleblower. The San Francisco Police Department said they found "no evidence of foul play," and the Chief Medical Examiner ruled his death a suicide. Balaji was born in Florida on November 21, 1998, in an Indian-American family. He grew up in Cupertino, California, where both of his parents worked in the technology industry. He began coding at age 11 using the children's programming tool Scratch, and built his own computer when he was 13. Balaji attended Monta Vista High School and was a finalist in the 2015–16 season of the United States of America Computing Olympiad. In 2017, he placed 7th in a Kaggle "Passenger Screening Algorithm Challenge" sponsored by the TSA, and won $100,000 in prize money. He won first place in the 2017 Pacific Northwest Regional and Berkeley Programming Contests, and placed 31st in the ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest 2018 World Finals. He wrote a paper on chip design at age 14. At 17, he took a gap year and worked as a software developer at Quora. After his gap year, Balaji attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned a BA in computer science. While in college, he interned at Scale AI in 2019. He joined OpenAI after graduating in 2021. John Schulman, a cofounder of OpenAI, recruited Balaji directly after college. Balaji worked at OpenAI for almost four years as an artificial intelligence researcher. Among other work, he helped collect and organize internet data used to train GPT-4, a language model behind the company's chatbot ChatGPT. He also worked on an earlier model called WebGPT. In an online eulogy, Schulman wrote that "Suchir’s contributions to this project were essential, and it wouldn’t have succeeded without him." Balaji left OpenAI in August 2024 after becoming disappointed with what he saw as the company's business practices. He said, "If you believe what I believe, you have to just leave the company." After leaving, he said he was working on "personal projects." According to an interview with his mother, he planned to start a nonprofit focused on machine learning and neuroscience. His mother also said, "He felt AI is a harm to humanity." In an October 23, 2024 New York Times interview, Balaji said that products like ChatGPT break United States copyright law because they are trained on the work of business competitors, and because the outputs of these chatbots can imitate and replace those products. He argued that ChatGPT and similar systems hurt the ability of people and organizations to make money from the works that are used to train the AI models. The New York Times article summarized Balaji's essay "When does generative AI qualify for fair use?", which he had published on his personal website earlier that week. In the essay, he used a mathematical analysis of outputs from chatbots such as ChatGPT and argued that they do not pass the four-factor test for determining fair use under U.S. copyright law. He also suggested that his argument could apply to other generative AI products, not just OpenAI's systems. At the time, OpenAI was already being sued for copyright infringement by several well-known authors and news organizations, including The New York Times. In a November 18, 2024 court filing, lawyers for The New York Times listed Balaji as one of several people who might have "relevant documents" in the copyright case against OpenAI. Several other people named in the filings were current or former OpenAI employees. Balaji said he was willing to testify against OpenAI. Unlike some other OpenAI whistleblowers, Balaji did not reveal any previously unknown internal information about the company. The New York Times article quoted Stanford University law professor Mark Lemley, who disagreed that generative AI services as described by Balaji clearly violate copyright law, and intellectual property lawyer Bradley Hulbert, who said new laws might be needed to decide the legal questions. Months after Balaji's death, which had drawn widespread public attention, Hulbert told Fortune that Balaji's essay "reads like the argument of a really smart non-lawyer who read up on the subject but does not have a thorough understanding." Another intellectual property lawyer, quoted anonymously by the magazine because of concerns about conspiracy theories connected to Balaji's death, said that Balaji's argument "misunderstands the law in some fundamental ways." OpenAI responded that its software is "grounded in fair use and related international copyright principles that are fair for creators and support innovation," and that it is "trained on publicly available data." Balaji's parents say they last heard from him on November 22, 2024. When he stopped answering text messages, they asked San Francisco police to check on him at his home with a well-being check. On November 26, 2024, police found Balaji dead in his apartment with a single gunshot wound to the head. He was 26 years old. The gun found at the scene was registered to Balaji, who had bought it in January 2024. On February 14, 2025, the San Francisco Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) released an autopsy report. It concluded that Balaji died from a single, self-inflicted gunshot wound on the same day that police discovered his body. Police reported that the only entrance to the apartment was locked with a deadbolt from the inside, and that Balaji had recently searched for information about brain anatomy on his computer. Toxicology tests showed alcohol, amphetamine and GHB in his system. Because of his role as a possible "custodial witness" in The New York Timess lawsuit against OpenAI, and his public claims that OpenAI violated AI copyright law and followed poor AI ethics practices, Balaji's death attracted major public and media interest. News coverage also highlighted his essay in which he laid out his legal arguments against OpenAI. Even though San Francisco authorities initially described Balaji's death as suicide, the circumstances and the lack of detailed information at first led to widespread speculation and conspiracy theories. Many online commentators claimed that Balaji might have been killed to stop him from testifying against OpenAI. Before the official autopsy was released in February, Balaji's parents publicly questioned the initial conclusion that he had killed himself. They began a public campaign to challenge what they saw as an incorrect ruling from San Francisco authorities. They said that he had been "cheerful" about two weeks before his death and pointed to the lack of a suicide note and what they described as "blood spatter anomalies" in his apartment. In December 2024, his parents announced that they had hired private investigators and ordered a second autopsy. They claimed that this autopsy suggested homicide, saying that Balaji was shot "in the back of the head from an angle at which he could not have shot himself." They did not release a copy of the report, and their lawyer said he "would not characterize it as conclusively proving murder". The official autopsy by the OCME described the bullet path as going from front to back and downward. Claims of foul play increased in visibility after Elon Musk (who has had public disputes with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman) replied to a social media post by Balaji's mother and wrote that the death "doesn't seem like a suicide." In January, Tucker Carlson discussed Balaji's death with his mother on his podcast. That same day, Silicon Valley Congressman Ro Khanna called for a "full and transparent investigation" into the case. San Francisco Supervisor Jackie Fielder also said she was "concerned" about the circumstances of Balaji's death. Fortune magazine described the parents' actions as part of a sincere attempt to understand what had happened to their only child. The magazine spoke with several of Balaji's friends, who shared the parents' confusion and grief. It quoted Daren Firestone, an "attorney who works regularly with whistleblowers," who said that whistleblowers can feel lonely and doubtful, face "enormous pressure," and may feel that the "world is against [them]." Fortune also pointed out that "Balaji wasn’t divulging any previously unknown inside information about the company" and, comparing the situation to the John Barnett case, said that the parents' campaign had helped drive more online speculation. As of April 2025, the official conclusion of the San Francisco Police Department and the San Francisco Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is that Balaji died by suicide from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Sudan (1973 – March 19, 2018) was a captive northern white rhinoceros who lived at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Laikipia, Kenya. He was known for being one of only three living northern white rhinoceroses in the world, and the last known male of his subspecies. Sudan was euthanised on March 19, 2018, after suffering from "age-related complications".

Sudhindra Thirta (31 March 1926 – 17 January 2016), also known as Shri Sudhindra Thirtha Swamiji, was an Indian Hindu religious leader. He was the legal and spiritual head (mathadipathi) of the Kashi Math and the twentieth successive person called the swamiji of guru parampara. He was born in Ernakulam, Kerala, India. Swamiji attained Moksha in Haridwar, India from renal failure on 17 January 2016 at the age of 89.

Sudhakar Chaturvedi (died 27 February 2020) was an Indian Vedic scholar, Indologist, and alleged supercentenarian. At the claimed age of 122 years, 313 days, some Indian newspapers reported him as the oldest Indian ever. One report also claimed an age of 121 in 2011, which would put his birth in 1890. Chaturvedi was a contemporary of Mahatma Gandhi, whom he first met when studying the Vedas in a gurukula in northern India. Chaturvedi died on 27 February 2020, at the claimed age of 122.

Sudhir Chakravarti (19 September 1934 – 15 December 2020) was an Indian anthropologist and essayist. He was born in Shibpur, British India. Chakravarti was known for his research works on Folk religion, Lalan Fakir and Cultural Anthropology in Bengal. He spent 30 years researching the folk culture by traveling to different villages all over the West Bengal. He was a professor of Bengali literature from 1958 to 1994. Chakravarti worked in Krishnagar Government College. He wrote and edited more than 85 books on many subjects like music, art, folk-religion, cultural anthropology. He was the editor of Bengali literary Magazine Dhrubapada. Chakraborty died on 15 December 2020 in Kolkata, India from a heart attack at the age of 86.

Susan Lillian "Sue" Townsend, FRSL (2 April 1946 – 10 April 2014) was an English novelist and playwright. She was best known as the author of the Adrian Mole books. Most of her works combined comedy with social commentary and also wrote purely dramatic works. She was born in Leicester, Leicestershire. Townsend was diagnosed with diabetes in the 1980s. She received a kidney from her elder son in 2009. She had a stroke in 2012. She died on 10 April 2014 at her home in Leicester after having another stroke. She was 68 years old.

Susan Ann "Sue" Lloyd-Roberts CBE (27 October 1950 – 13 October 2015) was a British television journalist. She worked for BBC programs and, earlier in her career, worked for ITN. Lloyd-Roberts died on 13 October 2015 at University College Hospital in London from leukemia, aged 64.

Sue Taylor Grafton (April 24, 1940 – December 28, 2017) was an American author. She mostly wrote detective novels. She was best known for her "alphabet series" of books, featuring the character Kinsey Millhone. The first in the series was "A" Is for Alibi (1982); the final was "Y" Is for Yesterday (2017). She also wrote screenplays for television movies. Crime writer Ross Macdonald was her biggest influence as a writer. Grafton was born in Louisville, Kentucky. Her father was crime writer C. W. Grafton (1909–1982). She was divorced twice and had three children. She was married to Steven F. Humphrey until her death. Grafton died of cancer on December 28, 2017 in Santa Barbara, California. She was 77.

Susan Povey FMedSci (1942 – 11 January 2019), also known as Sue, was a British geneticist. From 1970 to 2000 she was at the Medical Research Council's Human Biochemical Genetics Unit at the Galton Laboratory. She was a professor at University College London from 2000 to 2007, becoming Emeritus after retirement. She was chair of the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee from 1996 to 2007. Povey was elected a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences (FMedSci) in 2000. Povey died on 11 January 2019 at the age of 76.

Sue Ko Lee (March 9, 1920 – May 15, 1996) was a labor organizer with the Chinese Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Association. In 1938, she joined the longest strike in San Francisco’s Chinatown's (at the time) history. This strike was a fifteen week long strike against the National Dollar Stores factory. Lee and the other workers who striked were tired of the low wages and poor working conditions they were given. They did not have many job options to choose from, so were forced to take the work they could get at the National Dollar Stores factory. This was because many white owned businesses would not hire them due to the fact that they were Chinese American. She helped organize and lead the strike and delivered speeches. The Dollar Store Strike was successful, in part due to her efforts. The workers got a 5 percent raise, and the conditions in which they were working also started to improve. This strike directly impacted the workers at the National Dollar Stores factories. In addition, after the company closed, more companies, even those that were previously made up of only white people, were willing to hire Chinese Americans. After the strike, Lee also became a leader of the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union. Lee was born in Honolulu, Hawaii on March 9, 1920. She moved to Watsonville, California, as a child. She was the oldest of ten children. At eighteen, she married Lee Jew Hing. He was an immigrant from China. He worked as a bookkeeper for National Dollar Stores, causing Lee to eventually work at the same factory. Sue Ko Lee and Lee Jew Hing had two children together. Lee saved all of her memories, documents, and items from the strike in a scrapbook, and participated in an interview before she died. The interview and scrapbook helped give much of the currently known information about the strike. Lee died in El Cerrito, California on May 15, 1996.

Sugako Hashida was a Japanese scriptwriter. She was known for writing the NHK Asadora Oshin. She was thought to be Japan's most successful TV drama scriptwriter. She created Hashida Cultural Foundation. Her real name was Sugako Iwasaki. In 2020, she received the Order of Culture.

A suffragan bishop is a type of bishop in some Christian denominations. In the Catholic Church, a suffragan bishop leads a diocese that is part of a church province, which it is not the main diocese (usually led by the metropolitan archbishop).
